maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF AGREEMENTS WITH SIX PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF AGREEMENTS WITH SIX PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
I believe that hon. members will be interested to know that the federal government this morning entered into agreements with six provincial governments for the construction, under the terms of the Trans-Canada Highway Act passed by parliament last session, of the links of the trans-Canada highway through their respective provinces.
Contracts were signed with representatives of Ontario, Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The provinces with which an agreement was not signed were Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland.
Hon. members will recall that when the bill was being considered by parliament last session I informed the house of the government's view that the project would not be national in scope unless all provinces entered into the agreement, and that unless it were national in character the federal government would not be justified in participating.
However, in view of the fact that those provinces in which no such east-west highway exists have all signed the agreement, and having regard also to the fact that the implementation of the agreement with the
six provinces will result in a hard-surfaced) road from east to west across Canada, thereby in substance achieving the aim of the-act, it is the opinion of the government that-the people of Canada generally would approve-of having the project proceed in the six provinces with respect to which agreements have been signed. I am convinced, moreover, that it is only a matter of time until the remaining provinces will participate in the project.
I should like at this time to express the appreciation of the government for the wholehearted co-operation extended by the provincial ministers and officials concerned in the negotiations.
The agreement was signed on behalf of the province of Ontario by Hon. George H. Doucett, minister of highways and public works; of the province of Manitoba by Hon. E. F. Willis, minister of public works; of the province of British Columbia by Horn E. C. Carson, minister of public works; of the province of Prince Edward Island by the premier, Hon. J. Walter Jones; of the-province of Saskatchewan by Hon. J. Ti. Douglas, minister of highways and transportation; and of the province of Alberta by Hon. D. B. MacMillan, minister of public works.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I adjourned the debate on the 4th of April I was trying to explain to the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Major) and the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Gour) that the high price of grain should not be laid at the door of the western farmer. The hon. gentlemen know quite well that all grains are handled by the wheat board, as announced in the house a few days ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe).
Farmers in the east are seriously annoyed because of the prices they have to pay for feed grains. Before going further into that matter I want to make it perfectly clear to all those using feed grains that the western farmer has no intention of exploiting this market by holding grain at ridiculously high levels. He has far more sense than to do anything like that. I should like to direct attention to the fact that the floor prices of wheat, oats and barley today are $1.40, 65 cents and 93 cents per bushel respectively. Of course those prices are in store at Fort William; but the producer in the prairie

provinces actually receives approximately $1.20 for wheat, 55 cents for oats and 79 cents for barley. Freight and handling charges amount to approximately 20 cents in the case of wheat, 10 cents in the case of oats and 14 cents in the case of barley. Of course the farmer is entitled to any profit that may accrue from the sale of the grain by the wheat board after the crop season is over, by means of participation certificates.
Since hon. members from the east are accustomed to deal with wheat, oats and barley by the ton; let me put it in that form. At these prices the producer in western Canada is getting $39.60 per ton for wheat, $32.35 for oats and $33.18 for barley. So I do not believe hon. members who understand the growing of grain will consider for a moment that the western producer is getting too much, having in mind what he must pay for his implements and the materials that enter into his production costs.
One of the principal things the western producer wanted was a steady price, which would not only give him confidence to produce but would also give the purchaser of his produce grain at steady prices. That is why the farmers favour having the wheat board handle all grain, so that steady prices may prevail for both the producer and the consumer. But we have fluctuations from day to day, and complaints from consumers. What are the reasons for these fluctuations in grain prices? I do not know whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce can tell us, but certainly these prices should not be changing as they do. Evidently someone, through the speculative market, has been able to place those who require cash grain in a position where they must pay premiums of as much as 10 cents per bushel for oats and 35 cents for barley, in order to obtain their immediate requirements.
This additional cost to the eastern feeders does not necessarily mean increased prices to the western producers. It is much more likely to represent profit taken by speculators on the Winnipeg grain exchange. This is why we in the C.C.F. have always believed in the abolition of the speculative market. Let us look at what was said by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Gour) on April 4, as reported at page 1559 of Hansard:
Therefore I think it is my duty to urge our good friends, the grain growers of the western provinces, not to create such a bad situation for their friends, the farmers of the east, who after all are their best customers, because in the near future they will need them to buy their grain and it will be too late. Today the bulk car price for No. 3 C.W. oats is $76 a ton at stations in eastern Ontario less a subsidy of $6 per ton. Barley is about the same. At the present time farmers, dealers and co-operatives
The Budget-Mr. Bryce refuse to buy. It will mean less bacon, less cheese, less chickens, and so on. The quoted price for grain on July 31 last was $15 less per ton. Why do we not have the July price today? If we did, our farmers would buy, the western farmers would get their money more quickly, and the eastern farmers would keep on producing the food. It would not create this misunderstanding between eastern farmers who need the grain and western farmers. The western farmer needs the eastern farmer to buy his grain. We need the best friendship we can possibly have.
If you compare the amount the western farmer receives for his oats, about $32.35 a ton at the elevator, and the $76 a ton the hon. member says farmers in his constituency are paying, there is a big difference. To my way of thinking the difference is much too great. I agree that the eastern farmer is paying too much, but I am sure the hon. member will agree that the western producer is not receiving too much. The situation is much the same with respect to barley; but let us deal for a moment with oats, which at last week's prices would cost approximately $59 a ton at Fort William. The freight to points in the vicinity of Montreal or Ottawa would be an additional $2.40. Loading would cost $1.50. Bags would have to be provided, but, since they can be used several times, an allowance of $2 per ton for bags should be sufficient. This would give a total of $63.72 per ton at any point in my hon. friend's constituency. Taking the figure at an even $64, when my hon. friend pays $76 the difference is $12 a ton or $480 on a forty-ton car of oats. It would be a good thing if the eastern farmer would check into this and see if someone is not charging more than the traffic should have to bear. On Friday of last week I checked Ottawa prices and found that wheat, in bags to the farmer, was $74 a ton, oats were $70 and barley was $69. I also checked the Montreal figures and found that wheat was $71, oats $70 and barley $69.
Taking oats again as an example, the price at both Montreal and Ottawa was $70, which leaves a profit of $6 per ton for the handling of a ton of grain. In other words on a forty-ton car there would be an allowance of $240 for handling 800 bags of oats, which seems a good profit. I have known dealers in the west who were satisfied to handle oats at 10 cents a bag, and make money. Fluctuations in the market will also cause the dealer to charge the highest price in order to safeguard himself, but if we had steady set prices he could certainly cut down on his margin of profit.
As to the east and west being good friends, we just cannot afford to be anything else; we must be good friends. I think the

The Budget-Mr. Bryce Canadian Federation of Agriculture has done a wonderful job in getting both east and west to understand each other's problems, and I do hope that as the years go by we may understand those problems better and by doing so become better Canadians.
As reported at page 1560 of Hansard, referring to the farmers of the west, the member for Russell says:
I hope they will not ask again tor more money from the government or that they will not refuse to deliver their grain. Perhaps it is only natural to want to get another ten or twenty-five cents a bushel, but sometimes too much ambition is not good for you.
The farmers are not asking for more money from the government; far from it. What the farmer or producer has been doing is asking for steady prices based on his cost of production, which everyone will agree is fair. To the best of my knowledge he has not refused to sell his grain. But let us remember that barley and oats production is down about 70 million bushels from 1948-49, according to the figures of the Department of Agriculture, so there may not be much more oats to come, especially as hog production has increased by 20 per cent according to the latest agriculture figures. If the farmers are going to start feeding more hogs in the west, there will be less grain to come east-not because they do not want to send the feed, but because they intend to feed it themselves.
If the government, through the wheat board, can succeed in doing away with speculation in grain, feed can be sold more cheaply to the feeder in the east so that the poultry man or pig feeder would not need to pay $3.50 for a 100-pound bag of oats. Under order in council P.C. 5434, dated November 17, 1949, no dealer in eastern Canada needs to add any more than $2.40 per ton for freight to the price of feed grain. The order in council says:
The Minister of Agriculture is authorized to pay freight assistance . . .
Provided that such assistance shall be paid as follows:
(a) On all rail shipments from Fort William, Port Arthur or Armstrong, the payment shall be the sum of $6 per ton when the destination is within the Montreal freight rate zone, and the sum of $6 per ton plus the remainder of the actual through car lot rail freight charges to destinations beyond the Montreal freight zone, and the actual car lot rail freight charges, but not exceeding $6 per ton, to destinations in northern Ontario to which the local freight rate is less than the Montreal zone freight rate.
As a result of that concession by the government no dealer anywhere in eastern
'Mr. Bryce.]

Canada can charge up more than $2.40 for freight on the grain. The freight rate to Montreal is $8.40, but the Department of Agriculture pays $6 of that; so the dealer has only to add $2.40 to the price of feed, plus his expenses for handling.
Perhaps if I give a few points where feed is shipped, one will be able to understand how it works. Let us take the two points mentioned by the two gentlemen who complained about the expensive feed they had to buy. If we take Alexandria, Ontario, the freight rate from Fort William is 42 cents per hundredweight; that is $8.40 per ton. The government pays $6 of that. I have here, Mr. Speaker, a list of about ten points that I have taken. If we take Riviere du Loup, the freight rate is 60 cents per hundredweight, or $12 per ton; and the government pays $9.60. For St. John's, Newfoundland, the freight rate from Fort William is $1.31 per hundredweight, or $26.20 per ton; and the government pays $23.80. May I have your permission, Mr. Speaker, or the permission of the house to put on Hansard this table of rates for these ten points without reading it?

farmers in the west are not charging them too much for our feed grains. The price is fair and reasonable. I have shown that there is a margin of $240 per car on Montreal and Ottawa prices. Surely grain could be handled more cheaply than that. If the dealers cannot do better than that, 1 suggest to them that they should set up a co-operative and get service at -cost; then if you pay too much for your feed, you will get it back in patronage dividends. That is the solution to the problem: get your co-operative to handle your feed.
In concluding, I want to assure hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate on this subject of feed grain prices that the western producer is anxious to have the eastern trade, but he does not like to be accused of charging too much for his grain when that is not the case; and I hope I have proved to them that the producers are not getting too much. Even if the west again increases her hog production, there will always be in the west more feed grains than we can use. We realize that the eastern market is our best outlet for our feed grains, and we do not want to lose it. By order in council P.C. 5435, passed on November 17, 1949, the government has power to check the distribution of feed grain. The last paragraph of section 2 reads as follows:
Provided that, on all grains and feeds shipped and distributed in accordance with provisions hereof, evidence satisfactory to the minister is produced to show that the sale price to consumers of such products has been reduced by and takes into account the payment of freight charges as herein prescribed.
Perhaps the best thing to do is to have the government check the eastern prices. They are paying $6 to $23.80 per ton at different points to enable the feeder to get grain at his local point at a reasonable price in order to compete in the production of hogs, poultry and cheese. I am sure that all western farmers will support the eastern farmers in a demand for an inquiry into eastern feed prices. It
The Budget-Mr. Dechene would clear the air and expose anyone who is taking more profit than he deserves for the services he renders in the feed situation.

speechtext:
In asking you, Mr. Speaker, for the privilege of the floor this afternoon, I am speaking from your left:, for the first time in all these years, but it is, not because I have changed my political! allegiance.
I have no great message to bring to you, Mr;. Speaker, or to this house. I admit that I do not come into the arena to do battle with the great j ousters who have entered the debate already. I do not claim to have the qualifications or the ability to do so. I admit to you, sir, that I always hesitate to speak in this house, not from a false sense of humility but because I realize my weaknesses and my failings. But I do feel I am justified in seeking the attention of parliament for a short time this afternoon. I have that feeling after all these years, some thirty, as a representative of the people either in Alberta or here; and after nearly sixty years of residence in northwestern Canada, I cannot escape the conviction that I can bring to you and to the house a message from the pioneers who have done yeoman work in advancing the settlement of those great western plains and have created so much wealth for the rest of Canada.
A year ago we were asking the people of this, country to decide upon the government they wanted. No one was more pleased than I was,, sir, to witness the tremendous support that: the people of Canada gave to this government; and what a consolation it was, to those of us who felt that the Liberal party was the party that could give good government to this country, to see such an overwhelming, majority of the people give support to such a large number of representatives of that party. I was struck, sir, immediately by the ability displayed by those young and newer members, some of them not so young, but all new members in this house. I was greatly impressed by their knowledge, by their ability to express themselves as representing their constituencies and the people of Canada generally. I am prouder than ever to be a member of that group, almost two hundred, who are charged with the tremendous task of working for the welfare of the Canadian people.
Alberta, born lucky, Alberta, the best of all,
I believe, sir, is sitting as it were in the lap of the Rocky mountains, making "goo-goo" eyes at the man in the mountains but remaining true to the man on the plains, because he is such a good provider. Alberta has a lot to offer to the people of this country. It is as a pioneer in the province of Alberta that I

The Budget-Mr. Dechene again wish to bring to your attention, sir-and to ask for your support-the things that I believe we ought to do in order to bring more wealth out of that good country that God has made so rich.
I remember that at a convention I had the honour to address years ago-and, sir, will you let me repeat the thought that I had at that time-I spoke of the beauties, the possibilities, the wealth of the vast plains and the incredible amount of coal under our soil, the oil that I predicted thirty years ago would be found, as it is today, our great forests and magnificent rivers, our lakes teeming with fish, and our population, sir, still scant but coming from the best human stock that God has created. I said, and I repeat today, I thought that when the Lord, after having created the worlds, and thrown into space the suns, the planets and the comets, and all of those millions of worlds in limitless space, He decided on the seventh day to rest, and having cast a look upon the work that He had done He declared Himself satisfied. I am sure, sir, that at that moment He looked over the valleys of the province of Alberta, the great valleys of the Peace and the Athabasca rivers.
In speaking to you, sir, many years ago I said I believed that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was a coming man. After having spoken of the tremendous task .performed by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, I [DOT]expressed the thought that the gentleman who succeeded him was one of the most brilliant ; young men in the political life of Canada 'itswSay. That prediction has been fully justified.
The Prime Minister of this country, following the precedent established by the ex-prime minister, has recently recruited some younger members to the strength of his cabinet. As an old-timer in the house I welcome them and wish them success. I know that the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) will prove a great strength in this government. I have always admired him, ever since the first day I met him here after he had just come back from overseas bearing his glorious wounds received in battle on behalf of his king and country. I have always admired him as one of the typical, clever, able Ontario representatives, and I am pleased that the Prime Minister of this country saw fit to invite him to join the cabinet.
I wish the best to the hon. gentleman who has recently been called to the cabinet, the son of the man who made such an outstanding mark in the history of Canada, the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, who bore the mantle that Sir Wilfrid Laurier laid down in 1919. I know that he will occupy the position in the glorious tradition established in this house by
	|
his eminent father. I hope I shall be forgiven if I do not speak of any of the other members.
A moment ago I said I was pleased that Saskatchewan was again largely represented in this house by Liberals. I never could understand the attitude of the western farmers in 1945 toward the man who did more for them than any other man has done. In 1941, in the first bad year of the great war, when things were so gloomy and everything looked as if we might see for the first time in history the British commonwealth of nations and even the powerful United States defeated, when France had been knocked to its knees, I remember how satisfied we were, how proud we were, and how safe we felt in western Canada to have the business of agriculture in the hands of the Right Hon. James G. Gardiner who sits across from me this afternoon.
My statement to the people-there were only two of us from Alberta and two of us from Saskatchewan at that time-my statement to people of Alberta, to those who asked me questions, was: "Watch Jimmy Gardiner. You can't keep him down". And they did not, Mr. Speaker. He came back here with as good and as strong a following of first-class men to support him as he has ever had. My own province has sent down support in order to carry out the great public projects that are necessary to continue the development of this northern area for which I have worked all my life, sir, to the detriment of my own health, if I may speak of myself, and certainly to the detriment of my finances. Finances do not matter very much now; I shall not need them very long. In my speech this afternoon I hope I do not go over the time limit.
A few days ago I was reading the column of one of those columnists in Ottawa who know so much. I am always surprised by the tremendous knowledge they display- some of them concerning things they do not know much about. One of them proceeded to say that members of the House of Commons seem to feel that they have to take the full forty minutes allotted to them. There was nothing wrong with that statement -except that he should have noted that some members of the House of Commons, including the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), rarely speak more than once in a session, while others address the house hours and weeks. Indeed, I know some members of parliament, who do not sit far from me, who never miss an opportunity to speak in the house. They speak about everything they think about. They have not had one unuttered thought.

When I decided to take part in this debate I felt I could say something different, particularly after having witnessed the coal strike in the United States, which has led to the ruin-and I say this advisedly-of coal mining in my native province of Alberta. Do not forget that. We are hearing from the Labour-Progressive party and from others in protest against conditions in our coal mines, and this at a time when everything has been done to ruin coal mining in the United States. Today the people are turning to oil and other fuels. Can we blame them?
This is simply carrying on a policy which had its beginning during the last war, when thoughts nauseous and destructive came over from Russia to poison the minds of not only the people of Europe but those in this country. They are doing their work in this great free country, where there is so much to be done.
During holy week I attended church, as is my custom. On Good Friday I said to myself, "Here was a Man from Heaven, a Man who came to teach us how to live our lives, who suffered our suffering and offered His own life to redeem free men, and to open the door of the kingdom to the inhabitants of the earth, a kingdom from which otherwise they would be barred."
I am not a preacher, far from it. But my mind did turn to thoughts about this country and our people. This is the wealthiest country in the world, with more resources than we can dream of. It seems to me we have everything. And when the Creator had created that marvellous, that incredible thing, the human mind, He said that He had finished; and all those good things left were just scattered throughout North America, and particularly in Canada. We have blessings of all kinds-coal, forests, oil, everything we want.
What do we do with all this? Do we, sir, get together to enjoy them? Do we, sir, get together to develop them? Do we, sir, get together to do anything about these resources? No. We have witnessed people from other nations across the oceans come over with their prejudices. We have listened to appeals to greed, avarice, hatred, narrow-mindedness and intolerance. I am sick and tired of all these.
I was one of those few survivors of the Liberal party in my province in 1921. That is a long time ago. The whole campaign in those days was one of intolerance. I can remember a great preacher who came from
The Budget-Mr. Dechene across the line to tell us that this was a fight between autocracy and plutocracy; a fight with the masses.
We were told about capitalism, and to beware of the old parties. Yes, "Beware of the old parties!" Then later, in 1935, the new gospel was preached, when the United Farmers of Alberta had their turn. Then, in fifteen years they became an old party, and a new development came along. Again we heard, "Beware of the old parties", and the
U.F.A. was put out of office with that same cry. What things they promised; what things they said!
Is it proper for me to ask in this House of Commons today whether there is anything wrong with those things that are old? Religion is old, is it not? Yet, there is nothing wrong with it, is there? I said to the old and to the young in Alberta during that election campaign-and I make the same appeal today, regretting only that my voice is not loud enough to go all through this land -"No, do not despise the old." What lies beneath the white hair of those older members in the House of Commons? What lies in the breasts of all good people? The older ones have devoted their lives to their country to an extent greater than the younger. Those older people have had good experience.
What a wonderful book we have as our guide. Hon. members may send their sons and daughters to the best schools in the country-and there can be no doubt that we have great schools. We may send them to the best universities the country offers. They may come from those universities with enough degrees to fill a page. But they have not learned about that book. How often have we seen a boy come from his school, with all his knowledge and with the advantage of everything he has read, and with the intelligence to reach the heights, and to achieve success for himself, his family and his country, only to find himself faced with a situation he does not understand. He does not know how to face it because there was nothing in his books about it.
Where does he go? He goes to dad; the daughter goes to mother. His dad may not be able to read; but he and the mother have read that book. They have lived and struggled and they know what to do. They say, "My boy, go ahead; here is the way to fix it." Today I appeal to the young people to withstand those appeals to hatred, intolerance and prejudice, religious and otherwise. I detest and abhor such appeals. I appeal to the young homesteaders on the shores of Cold lake for instance in the northern part of my constituency who have been approached by these splinter parties, who are responsible for

The Budget-Mr. Dechene their present uncertain state of mind. They urge them to look at the big money being made in Montreal and elsewhere.
That is not the appeal I make to them. I say to the hon. members of the House of Commons and, through them, to the people of Canada, that a man developing a homestead away up there on the fringe of the northern section of our country is performing just as useful a task as is the president of the Bank of Montreal. The man up in the wilds attending his traps is just as useful, because he is part of the great machinery of democracy. We hear from these small parties appeals to shallowness and intolerance. But they should not monkey with the democratic machine; it is easily put out of order.
Every cog and every wheel is important.
I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that when you were a boy you did what I did: you took a clock apart to see what made it tick-and then you had some wheels left over, and the clock never worked again. In a great democracy every wheel and every cog has its place. The trapper, the fisherman, the farmer, the rancher, the small merchant, the coal miner, the labouring man, each has his place. He belongs and if you put him out of that place then the machine ceases to operate.
May I be allowed to take up the time of the house again in making an appeal I have made before. I am not at all satisfied with the results of my efforts in drawing attention to the need of railway construction in the northern parts of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. I know it is not popular to advocate things of this kind and we shall be told by Montreal that there is no money. Let me place before the house some of the aspects of this situation. Let me say to the directorate of the Canadian National Railways that we are not asking for any branch lines. If there is any possible way of waking them up in Montreal, I want to do it. I ask the privilege of again taking up the time of this house because we are bound that something shall be done.
I can recall that plans were made for this construction when I was a local member. Many years ago the people in the north country thought they were going to get a new artery of transportation which would connect with Winnipeg and the head of the lakes at the east and with the Hudson Bay railway, thus giving them two routes over which to send their surpluses to the markets of Europe. There was also to be an outlet to the west coast through the country represented by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray).
This is not a new plan. We are not asking for a branch line. What we are asking for will not cost the people of this country one


dollar because there are tremendous resources in this north country. I understand that the new president of the Canadian National Railways is soon going west and I hope he will find it possible to visit that part of the country and not just stay around Edmonton and the cities. He should see the vast possibilities that are in the north country, the great resources that will make this line pay a profit for the benefit of the people of the whole country.
I would not be taking up the time of this house if I were not absolutely convinced of the justice of the representations I am making this afternoon on behalf of these people. Let me say to the Canadian National Railways that it is not a question of money. We were told that there would be no money for the building of these branch lines, but it is not a question of money. It is a question of keeping a promise and paying a debt of honour. Surveys were made of a line from Battleford to the country which I represent, to be continued then by the Canadian Pacific along the north shore of the Beaver river. This was to be a joint undertaking of the two great transportation companies. The Peace river country was to be joined to the Northern Alberta railroads which have recently been acquired by the two companies.
Plans were prepared and tenders called for, at least for the construction in the part of the country which I represent. A beginning was made at both ends. The Canadian Pacific built west from Prince Albert and the Canadian National was building from Edmonton north-easterly, and they were to meet at a point some twenty miles east of the boundary of Saskatchewan. The Canadian Pacific had running rights over 55 miles of the Canadian National line until they reached Cold Lake.
As I say, contracts were let and millions of dollars were spent. As I stated before in this house, in 1932 the Canadian National paid a large sum to the contractor to be permitted to cancel his contracts. Thousands of men were looking for work along the line right through to the north.
The other day the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), referring to what I said last fall, asked why the Liberal government had not done anything from 1935 until 1940. The hon. member is a schoolteacher and he should be possessed of some information. He knows that in 1935, 1936, 1937 and 1938 the government of Alberta defaulted on their obligations to the extent of over $20 million. A blot was placed on the escutcheon of Alberta which it has taken decades to erase.

It may be; I do not know because I never read it, but if the editorial contains what he says it did then it is just a rag. He quoted the editorial as stating:
It was during the Borden administration, when the Alberta government was Liberal and so was the Senate. The Alberta government, it seems, wanted to give the Shell Oil Company exclusive oil rights for the whole province in return for a payment of $5,000. But it didn't have the power to do so, so it asked1 the federal government to give it that power.
I was well acquainted with the premier of the province of those days, a man who later came to Ottawa and served as minister of the interior, a man who represented his country with dignity and with honour, a man whose honesty and integrity have never been questioned, a man who never heard about any such thing. Can you imagine men like the Hon. Archie McLean, the Hon. John R. Boyle, or the Hon. J. L. Cote, trying to sell the oil rights of Alberta for $5,000? The thing was so ridiculous that I did not reply to it at the time.
I know what happened at that time. Representations were made by representatives of the Shell Oil Company-I am sure the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) will remember the instance-to try to get the odd section or portions of land in the Northwest Territories. We had nothing whatsoever to do with it at Edmonton. Nobody else was ever consulted. Talk about a falsehood! There is one that the hon. member for Red Deer peddled on the floor of the house to try to soil the reputation of men who served in better years and who gave the best of their lives to their province and their country.

I know you know all about it. It was up in the Northwest Territories and we had no jurisdiction in Alberta. We could not do anything even if we had wanted to. Twice it was denied in this house when I said, Mr. Speaker, that at least a royalty should be paid to the owners of the surface rights when oil is found under their land. In that same speech the big voice from Red Deer proceeded to refer to what has been paid by way of damages to some farmers for entry on their land or compensation of it. That was not initiated by the government of Alberta. The law of recompense and reward or compensation for using surface rights for public works, roads, railways or any other communication is as old as this House of Commons. A man cannot stop a railway company from proceeding over his land, but if he is not satisfied with the price offered he goes to arbitration and the price is fixed for the land used. That is what is happening in Alberta in the oil game.
We are told that this or that man received $1,100. I may have said "land" last fall and of course that was picked up right away, but I meant oil rights. Just across the line from this certain man the oil rights were sold a few days later for $1,125,000 in cold cash. Who gets this money? Not the farmer. The hon. member quoted further from the editorial in that same Calgary rag as follows:
It is unfortunate that a man of the stature of Mr. J. M. Dechene, Liberal M.P. for Athabaska-
I thank him for the compliment.
-in northern Alberta, should be so far off the beam on this matter of oil royalties. In parliament, the other day, he said the oil belonged "to the people, not to the provincial government," . . .
Then the editorial went on to ask whether the provincial government was going to be deprived of revenue for the sake of a few farmers in the north country. This is great reading for the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), where oil can and is being found almost everywhere. It is great reading for the people of the constituency of Battle River (Mr. Fair), the people of the constituency of Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas), and for all the people from Red Deer north. The farmers are told that they are not going to get their rights, that they are not entitled to any benefit for the wealth that God has put under their soil, because a few people think the money should be spent to build roads around Banff and other parts of the province.
I stand on the most solid ground because I made a motion to that effect. Some thirty years ago before any oil was found I saw that there was great wealth in the province of Alberta and I made a motion asking that

we should return the mineral rights to the owners of the soil. So much has been alienated since that it cannot be done now. They are finding wealth worth $1 million, $500,000, $100,000 every day throughout that district and right up into the Northwest Territories. I want the farmers, the men who went there with their wives and children, the men who built the schools and conducted the municipalities, the men who built the roads, chopped down the timber and trees and developed the land, to receive a royalty. If they are not entitled to a royalty on the wealth that God has placed under their feet then there is something wrong with the mentality of the governments of this country.
I wish I were a younger man. I would be willing to wage a campaign on this issue, but not for political purposes. I have not much to do now with politics. I know my number will soon be up, and that is the reason why I thought I might take a little longer of your time. I have said before and I want to repeat that, with the exception of the holy orders, there is nothing more sacred than the life of a man who devotes his best to the service of his country. There is nothing more noble in a democracy than to represent the people and to do everything in one's power in order that the people may be more prosperous and that one may be of some benefit to them.
As I speak to you this afternoon my thoughts go to the farmers of northeastern Alberta for the reason that Providence has not smiled upon us in the last two years. If it were not for the beneficial laws administered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) there would be actual suffering because last year's crop was extraordinarily bad. Yet our farmers can carry on. They are now preparing the seeds for another crop, and my last word is a prayer to Providence to bless their efforts and send the usually abundant rains of northern Alberta so that the land may smile again.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reviewing the budget for 1950 one cannot help being struck by two very remarkable features, particularly when comparing it with budgets which have gone before.
The first feature is the very material change in outlook on the part of the government with respect to tax reductions and revenue requirements for the future, as compared with the forecasts in the 1949 or election budget; and, secondly, the billion dollar complex that now dominates the thinking of the government and its ministers. As to the first, we remember the rosy optimism and sweeping generosity with which the tax cuts were

made in the budget of 1949, a generosity and optimism which seemed to take no thought for the future or, if it did, took thought only as far as June 27, and contained no suggestion that after that date there would be stern realities to be faced. Indeed, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the whole cabinet seemed like a man on a drunken spending spree. This is not such a far-fetched statement as it may seem, because in fact the government had been saving up for this election spree for some time. One has only to remember the budget presented by the same Minister of Finance in May, 1948. At that time employment and revenues were at approximately the same high levels as in 1949; yet the tax reductions were doled out, to say the least, with a cautious hand. Of course in 1948 the minister knew when the election was going to be held; and of course, in spite of his lip service to the theory of cyclical budgeting, he could not resist the temptation to save up one year, then give away what he had saved up for an election budget in the following year.
Therefore in 1948 we find him uttering words of caution; we find him referring to the heavy responsibility with which the people of Canada have entrusted him, and to the danger of approaching his budget problems in a short-sighted manner. If we look at page 4063 of Hansard for May 18, 1948, we see that he told us in very solemn tones, and I quote his words-
We must look further into the future than this year.
Most of us at that time thought the minister was looking into the future solely with concern for the fiscal policies of Canada as a whole. However, in the spring of 1949 we found that the future the minister had in mind was the future of the Liberal party, and the election requirements of that party. When we came to 1949 we found that the future requirements of Canada, which in 1948 had led him to adopt such a solemn and cautious tone, were thrown out the window in favour of the political requirements of the government. In 1948 the minister said, at the same page of Hansard:
Now is the time to lay the foundation for employment budgets in future, while fighting inflation at present.
At that time he should have been saying, as in fact he really had in mind, "Now is the time to lay the foundation for election budgets in future, while hiding the facts at present." So in 1948 the minister saved his funds for the election budget of the following year, and in 1949 the government went on its spree. Now, in 1950, it is nursing its sore head. We had a black budget in 1948; we had an election or spree budget in 1949;
The Budget-Mr. Fulton now in 1950 we have the hang-over budget. This year the government is like a man nursing a sore head, and the Minister of Finance is the solemn chemist behind the counter doling out the aspirins.
It is no wonder the government finds itself with this hang-over this year. All the ministers seem to have fallen into the habit of spending millions and billions, then waking up the next morning faced with the painful reality of having to raise the money to meet their expenditures. A man under the influence soon gets a billion dollar complex, only in this case the influence is not that of liquor but of power. The billion dollar complex is a serious matter, because unfortunately it is not their own but the country's money that the government is spending. So we have the Minister of Finance telling us this year that none of his successors will ever be able to contemplate a budget of less than approximately $2,400 million a year. We have the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) graduating from the million dollar mentality to the billion dollar mentality. It used to be "What's a million?" This year it is, "What's a billion?" The only people and the only industries that count with this government after its fifteen years in power apparently are those whose revenues run into the hundreds of millions. No longer is the little man or the little industry of any apparent importance to the government. We remember that the other day when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was presenting his review of affairs for the year and discussing the trade prospects of Canada, he brushed aside the whole apple industry because, he said, "We are talking billions and my hon. friend talks about apples." You see, Mr. Speaker, the total turn-over of the apple industry is less than $100 million, and apparently it does not count in the scheme of things of this government, which does not speak of anything less than billions.
Turning to a more detailed consideration of the budget as we find it this year, again two salient features emerge from an analysis of the minister's remarks. The first is that in the opinion of the Minister of Finance we have reached rock bottom in the reduction of expenditures. Arising out of this is his conclusion that the only way to obtain tax reductions at the present time is to eliminate some essential services. The minister said, at page 1215 of Hansard:
It is only by reducing government activities or social service payments that any major reductions can be made.
But the point of departure between the government side of the house and this side is that whereas this inescapable conclusion seems to produce an atmosphere of defeatism

The Budget-Mr. Fulton in the minister, we on this side are convinced that in fact reductions in expenditure are possible and thus tax reductions are possible without interfering with any vital service, such reductions being made by a pruning of non-essential and non-productive government activity. Indeed, it seems that the minister's defeatism in this respect is actually charged with most unfortunate consequences, because he has made it very clear in his budget speech that the official attitude is that expenditure cannot be further reduced. From now on, therefore, every minister, every government official will be encouraged to relax and conclude that no further inefficiency or duplication need be sought out and eliminated, that the seal of official government approval is placed upon swollen and top-heavy expenditures of $2,400 million a year. To the taxpayers of Canada who have to produce the money to meet those expenditures, however, such a defeatist attitude is entirely unacceptable; and it is certainly wholly rejected by the official opposition.
The other and even more alarming salient feature of the minister's budget address arises from the fact that if we accept his statement as final we must come to the inescapable conclusion that increases in taxes in the immediate future are inevitable. To a people suffering from a cost of government out of all proportion to the services the government renders and the productive value of those services, to a people labouring under a cost of living which has increased by six points in a year over a level already too high, such a conclusion and such a forecast are entirely unsupportable. Fortunately an analysis of the facts indicates that the conclusion and forecast are also totally inaccurate.
The Minister of Finance sees no room for leeway. He sees no possibility of allowing for tax reductions by a reduction in nonessential expenditures. To him the only prospect is increased taxation. At page 1216 of Hansard he said:
In considering proposals for further major increases in our expenditures . . . we must be ready to balance them with increased taxes.
And again:
If the expenditure is worth while, it should be provided for by new or increased taxes or charges . . .
I ask the house to consider the implication of those words in the light of the minister's earlier statement which appears on page 1215:
As already announced, there will be another conference with the provinces this fall, and whatever may be the eventual outcome of that conference, I think it is fair to assume that its decisions will not result in a lessening of the net burden on the federal budget.


There the minister very deliberately forecasts the possibility of substantially increased expenditures being agreed to this fall. The only and inescapable conclusion from this carefully-worded speech is that the minister regards higher taxes in the very near future as inevitable. It does not seem to the minister that we have arrived at the point where he should say to the house and to the country that the time has come when we have to choose between higher taxes or less government spending. He has said that we cannot have more spending without more taxes or a reduction of services, but he has not taken the other logical step and said that we cannot have less taxes without less spending and he has not taken the next step and said, "And we can have less spending."
We can, Mr. Speaker, have less spending. While I totally reject the minister's assumption that higher taxes are inevitable, I agree- as I think we all must-that the tremendous twofold problem facing this country and facing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is this:	How are we going to reduce taxes
at the present time; or, alternatively, how are we going to provide for increased expenditures which will arise out of the increased social services which the government is now contemplating, and for the increased activities in developing our resources, without a substantial and unacceptable increase in taxation?
A consideration of this problem prompts us further to agree with the minister that these things cannot be done and increased taxation cannot be avoided unless there is some reduction in expenditure. But that is as far as we can agree with the minister. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and I ask all members of the house to consider whether they can seriously support the proposition that, with expenses running ait the present time at the rate of $2,400 million a year, there is no room for reduction in expenditure without actually interfering with essential services.
The minister, of course, has taken the definite position that such reductions are impossible and he has in fact challenged the opposition to show where such reductions can be made. I am sure that he intended that challenge to be taken seriously. I at any rate take it extremely seriously because I believe that it is only by meeting that problem and finding where reductions can be made that we can reduce expenditures and thus relieve the tax burden on the Canadian people. For my part I assume in the same way that the minister himself will take seriously our efforts to show where reductions can be made and that, if the proof is given, or if concrete suggestions are made, he will take them in that spirit and that all

members of the house will take them in the same spirit so that we can, as members of parliament and as servants of the people of Canada, together and in co-operation, set about reducing this enormous burden which is placed on the people of raising the money to meet the current level of expenditures.
Unfortunately, we are denied one method by which we might be able to arrive at suggestions for economy. I refer of course to the requests which have been made for committees to consider the various activities of government departments. I really believe that such committees reviewing not so much- or at least not only-the policies of the various departments, but reviewing the details of the proposed expenditures of the departments, could not fail to find places where there is room for a substantial reduction in those expenditures. For the time being at any rate this method is denied to us, although I hope that the government will reconsider the matter before another session, because I believe the seriousness of the problem and the urgent necessity of reducing expenditures warrant the trial of this method.
Here perhaps one should just refer to the statements made recently by the Auditor General in the other place when he said that the volume of government business had grown to such an extent and is of such complexity that the public accounts-that is, the estimates of the current year-are now placed before parliament in such a way that it is impossible to get a clear and concise picture of just what we are about. If it is impossible to get that picture, then certainly one is greatly handicapped at the outset in trying to make any concrete suggestions for reduction in expenditures.

We must therefore at the present time find methods other than this committee method, and I intend to suggest certain specific methods by which expenditures can be reduced.
Here I should like to pay tribute to the work of the treasury board. Treasury board is not always popular, but I believe that the country owes a large debt to it because under the system which the government
The Budget-Mr. Fulton insists upon following at the present time, when committees to review estimates are denied, the treasury board is virtually the only watchdog with any inside knowledge which stands between the people of Canada and an even greater level of expenditure than that which we now have.
The minister has in the past described how treasury board does its best to keep expenditures to a minimum. We would not be grateful if we did not express our appreciation of this work. But under the present system and with the present volume of expenditure and the present competition between departments for funds, I do not believe that treasury board can do the job alone. One has only to consider the course of expenditures over the past few years. Each minister naturally enough believes that his own department is the most important one-and the same is true of deputy ministers-and that unless he gets all the money he possibly can for his department, he will not be doing a good job for his department and for the country. There is therefore tremendous competition for increases in grants to the departments when they are preparing and presenting their estimates. I am quite sure that the time arrives when the pressure is such that even with treasury board standing in the way as doggedly as it can, yet with the department pressing for the grant to be made or the expenditure to be authorized, treasury board goes as far as it can go but finally says, "All right; you can have what you had last year but no more."
That is probably a last-ditch stand and even that is a great service to the people. But we need a far more detailed analysis of our problem than that. We need an analysis not so much of how to prevent expenditures from rising as of how to bring expenditures down-how to reduce expenditures from their present level. What is needed is someone with authority to apply the axe; I do not mean someone to apply the axe indiscriminately but someone to say which expenditures are really essential and which are not.
I recall that in the budget debate of 1947 I suggested that such a method might be found in the setting up of a budget committee, a committee of experts whose recommendations would be of a substantial nature, with authority to examine the estimates before they are approved and presented to the house, to say which items are essential and which are not. I will not repeat at this time the details of the suggestion which I made then, but I repeat the suggestion; and

I am glad to have the minister's questions, but I do not think it is necessary to repeat the details here. They will be found in the budget debate of 1947. That is not the purpose of my suggestion at all. Such a committee would ascertain which expenditures are really necessary, would help to eradicate duplication, waste and extravagance, and would be in a position to recommend, as between proposed expenditures and proposed increases, which ones should be granted, which ones would be more advantageous to the country, in the long run, as revenue-producing projects with a view to the ultimate increase of our gross national revenue.

There are further concrete proposals which I wish to make now. An examination of the detail of the estimates cannot fail to suggest that we are spending far more than is absolutely necessary under certain headings. I have selected what-did I hear my hon. friend ask a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad he asked the question, which one, because I have selected three typical ones. I am not suggesting they are exclusive because in fact I think they are typical. I think that any further inquiries along this line could elicit other useful information and establish that there are other expenditures that could be reduced. The three that I have chosen are: first, publicity, advertising and public information services; second, sundries, and third, travelling expenses. Here, Mr. Speaker, again I emphasize that we are faced with the necessity of making a choice, and the choice, as I have said, is not between whether we are going to have increased expenditures or increased taxation, the choice as I see it is between, on the one hand, continuing to spend at the present rate with the absolute certainty that that rate will increase, and, on the other, reducing expenditures so that we can in fact reduce taxes. If we approach the problem with that choice in mind and if we make the choice, then I certainly suggest to hon. members, and I am sure they will agree with me, that the astounding figures which we are spending, or proposing to spend this year under these three headings, can be substantially reduced.
Under the first heading of publicity, advertising and information, we find that the government proposes to spend this year a total of $6,064,775, an increase of over $266,000 over last year. There are 62 separate items in the details of the estimates for government publicity and information services. And these are just the details that I have been able to pick out, the details which are shown in the estimates. I refer, for instance, to the Department of National Defence, where I could not find in my somewhat rapid survey of the estimates any separate items for publicity. And yet we all know, for it is an established fact, that that department spend large sums on public information services. In this and the following matters I am not suggesting that none of these expenditures is essential or necessary; but I am certainly suggesting that we do not need to spend $6 million on government advertising and publicity. I believe if we make the choice I referred to we can get along on half that amount. I believe if we carried further on to the next logical
tMr. Fulton.]

step we would say, we are going to get along with half that amount, and that is all we are going to give you to do the job with.
In this connection I would refer to the suggestion I made in 1947 in dealing with the same matter. If it is stated, as it has been stated, that some information with reference to what the departments are doing is essential-and I am prepared to accept that statement-I suggest that the government should consider setting up a bureau of publicity in connection with the work of the various departments to control that competition between departments which inevitably and invariably, in government, results in increasing expenditures. In exactly the same way as we formerly set up the bureau for translations and the bureau of printing, whose objects were to reduce the over-all expenditures under those headings, so I think we can set up a bureau of publicity, give it half the amount we are now being asked to vote, and tell it to do the job-and we would still have all the government publicity we need, and more.
Next we come to the heading of sundries. These are variously described in the items as "sundries", "miscellaneous" or "contingencies", or any one of a variety of equally delightful and vague general terms that one would care to mention. What they amount to, Mr. Speaker, is nothing more or less than a sort of grab bag or petty cash account for the various departments. It is the loosest and sloppiest method of accounting that I have ever seen. I know it is true that all bookkeeping systems, all office systems, require an item for petty cash; but you and I, Mr. Speaker, run our books on the basis of keeping the amount in the petty cash down to the very minimum. What the government does, however, amounts in a sense to an open-end or blank-cheque spending account. We find in the estimates for this current year that the government proposes to spend under this heading of sundries no less than $17,586,227. There are 281 separate items in the detail of the estimates for sundries. Again I am not suggesting that no sundry accounts or petty cash accounts, if you like, should be permitted, but I do say that it is the most careless method of bookkeeping, when it is totalled up to $17 million over-all, and we can do our accounting better than this. I suggest that we can get along with not more than half this amount for sundries.
I should like to refer Your Honour to some of these details in the departmental spending on sundries, as I have gathered them from the estimates. They are as follows: for the Department of Agriculture the total this year is $198,000. I am just giving the round figures
The Budget-Mr. Fulton at this time. Citizenship and Immigration, $242,000; Finance, $219,000, a nice petty cash amount for the Minister of Finance and his departmental officials without any necessity for accurate accounting-

speechtext:
It will take a lot of explaining why we need to spend $17 million on sundries when we could get along with half of it. Remember, sundries is not the only general item in the estimates. There are such items as printing and stationery, telephone and telegraph, office equipment and all these other items. Then at the end we find this huge open petty cash account for sundries. Then we find other departments such as the Department of Transport with an item of $703,000 for sundries and so on.
The third heading to which I referred is that of travelling expenses. Again I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that in all these matters I have taken only the items which are revealed in the details of the estimates. From what I have been able to gather I would say that there are many other items under all these headings which are not shown as such in the estimates. I have taken only those that are shown. To come to the travelling expenses which are shown, one finds that there are 270 separate items in the details of the estimates for a total of $25,914,000, or nearly $26 million for travelling expenses. I should point out that one of the largest is in the Department of National Defence where you find that travel and transportation, freight and express are lumped together. Even assuming that only half of the total of $14 million shown in the Department of National Defence for this item-assuming that half of that-would be straight travelling expenses, that would still be $7 million, so that the total for travelling expenses on that assumption would still be about $18 million.

The Budget-Mr. Fulton
The total expenditure under these three headings alone-publicity, sundries and travel expenses-shown in this year's estimates amounts to $49,565,052. Again let me say that I am not suggesting immediately that this is all unnecessary. Unfortunately we have been refused committees, and we are therefore not in a position to know what is necessary and what is not. But I do say that it is not all necessary, and that the estimates will be subjected to the closest possible scrutiny in committee of the whole and unless satisfactory explanations are given in detail as to the necessity for these amounts then reductions will be moved.
I would also say without any hesitation that in the absence of explanations, which at the moment I cannot foresee, we could, if we were determined to do so, get along in this country with only half of that expenditure under these three headings alone. If we did that we would save a total of about $24,500,000. In connection with the publicity item, as I have said before, some may be necessary. A good deal of travelling may be necessary. Some discretion to the departments under the heading of sundries or contingencies is probably necessary. But in connection with publicity we could save money by setting up a publicity bureau, give it half of what we are spending now, and do the job with that half. We would have all the publicity we need. And so in connection with other items we could get along, if we made up our minds to do so, with about half of what we are spending now.
I should like to give the house some examples of departmental spending on travelling expenses. These are the figures:
Department of	Agriculture	 $2,148,000
Department of Citizenship and Immigration	 750,000
Department of	Fisheries	 676,000
Department of National Health and Welfare	 774,000
Department of	Transport	
1,038,000Department of	Veterans Affairs

These are only some of the departments picked at random. So I put forward the suggestion, with the utmost seriousness, that we could reduce our expenditures this year by $24,500,000 if we only cut out half what is proposed to be spent on these three items. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will not tell me that this is an insignificant saving when we are dealing with $2,400 million; I hope that even his billion-dollar mentality will appreciate the fact that a reduction of this amount, or indeed of one million dollars, will directly affect the amount of taxes paid by every Canadian.
A reduction of $24,500,000 is a most substantial item. I would point out that it is iMr. Fulton.]

as much as the total reduction given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his 1948 budget, on the income tax and sales tax reductions combined. To put it another way, $24,500,000 is as much as the total reduction in the retail purchase tax, gasoline tax and amusement taxes combined in the 1948 budget. Those were substantial reductions- at least so the minister said when he made them in 1948; and a reduction of this amount this year would bring a very substantial measure of much-needed relief to every Canadian taxpayer.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize that we are not setting ourselves up in judgment in saying that this or that expenditure can be eliminated entirely. What I am saying is that here are three typical items the expenditure of which does not of itself and by itself produce revenues for the Canadian people. I am suggesting that substantial economies, at least 50 per cent, could in most cases be made if we decided that we must make them, without in fact hurting the national economy or producing inefficient government service.
I believe the time has come when we must choose: we must face the decision, do we want more publicity or more pensions? In fact we must face the decision: do we want to spend as much on travelling expenses as we are now for government officials, or do we want to reduce taxes? Do we want a $17 million petty cash account or sundry account or do we want to cut it substantially and leave leeway for some more productive expenditure, or for further reductions in income tax in the future?
I believe we should decide in favour of the reduction in expenditure and the things that it will make possible by way of tax reduction. I believe the estimates for this year should be reduced accordingly; and if the Minister of Finance is serious, as I am quite confident he is, in his suggestion that the time has come to make these decisions, then I hope that he will agree and will lend his support to our efforts to bring about these savings.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to follow the line pursued by the previous speaker, except to say that while I agree with him that we need to be careful about the money we spend in the country, I would say that it would be a good thing for him to give a little attention to this general question: Canada since 1938 has more than doubled her production. She now is producing by way of $16 billion worth of goods a year; and she expects to be able to produce $16,250 million this year.

Judging by Canadian resources, I find it difficult to believe that we cannot double our production in the next twelve years, as we did in the last twelve. If brilliant young men of the type represented by the hon. member who has just taken his seat would devote their attention to the question of how to turn that full production into well-being of the Canadian people, they would not be cheeseparing, cutting off a little here and a little there. They would really open their eyes as to what could be in the future in a country so abundantly blessed with resources and the ability to transform those resources into the goods and services necessary for mankind.
