speechtext:
Widespread interest has developed in an event which took place about 8 p.m. on the night of April 12 in the Quebec city of Shawinigan Falls, with a population of about 25,000. All parties concerned will desire that the essential facts be
24. 1950
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore set down where they can be preserved for all to see, so as to avoid distortion of any point whatsoever in the future.
The implications and repercussions of this occurrence will disturb the peace of mind of any person anxious to make provision for peace, order and good government in Canada in time to come.
In order to set down these facts as dispassionately as possible, I believe it would be well to place on record the report appearing in the Montreal Daily Star of April 13, 1950. This newspaper is published in the same province, and not far from where the incident occurred. It states:
Shawinigan Mob Wrecks Christian Brethren
Chapel
1,500 Rioters Terrorize Protestant Sect Group And Tear Up Bibles and Prayer Books
An angry, gesticulating, taunting mob which ranged in size throughout the evening from 200 to 1,500, last night completely smashed the meeting place of a Christian Brethren group in Shawinigan Falls, keeping 27 persons penned up in an upstairs flat for two and a half hours.
Shawinigan Falls is 21 miles north of Three Rivers, Quebec, which is 76 miles east of Montreal.
All furniture, including the pulpit, was broken in the store which was used as a chapel by the small Protestant sect, and bibles and hymn books were taken into the street, torn to shreds and scattered in the gutters.
The mob was composed of men, women and children. Stones, empty bottles, ice and even eggs were thrown into the hall for an hour from 9 to 10 p.m. The plate glass windows of the store were smashed. At 10 p.m. part of the crowd made their way into the chapel and began to demolish everything they could lay their hands on, including the electric fixtures.
Building Was Used For Regular Services
The building which was assaulted is located at 32 Fourth street, and is used regularly for Sunday and week-day meetings by the eight families who compose the Christian Brethren Church in Shawinigan Falls.
An Evangelistic sect, the Christian Brethren have twenty congregations scattered throughout the province. They have no ordained ministers, but are led by "evangelists"-laymen who are called to the work but who are paid no salary.
According to Benoit Mongrain, a wheel-chair paralytic, who owns the building, about twenty brethren were in the "store" chapel when the stoning began. Several were women.
Although he is not a member of the sect himself, Mongrain invited the group to take shelter in his tenement home above the store. There the brethren group and the Mongrain family, composed of Mr. and Mrs. Mongrain and their five children, were held virtual prisoners from 9 to 11.30 p.m.
At that time a detachment of the Shawinigan police escorted the brethren out of the Mongrains* flat.
The brethren were led by Evangelist Paul Boeda, who could not be reached by telephone this morning at two locations where he is ordinarily available.
The night-shift squad of ten policemen of the Shawinigan force arrived on the scene early in the evening but made no arrests.
Mayor Frangois Roy said he was at a theatre performance and heard of the mob assault only

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore when he emerged at 11 p.m. He said he arrived on the scene at 11.30 p.m. when "everything was quiet."
He said that apparently the Shawinigan police had found that they "could do nothing" to stop the stoning of the building, but that they "protected those who were inside the flat."
Mayor Hoy stressed that none of the brethren suffered bodily harm.
While the stoning of the brethren meeting place was going on Mr. Boeda placed a telephone call from the Mongrain flat to Doctor Arthur C. Hill, of Sherbrooke, chairman of the executive committee of the Christian Brethren Church of Quebec.
The evangelist's first excited report was at 9 p.m., and he called again at 10 p.m. After that nothing was heard from Mr. Boeda, and even this morning when Doctor Hill arrived in Montreal, no success was obtained in reaching the pastor by telephone.
Doctor Hill immediately boarded a train for Shawinigan Falls to conduct a personal investigation.
He said that he also spoke on the telephone to chief of police Napoleon Longval last night while the assault was in progress, and that the chief assured him that everything was being done to keep order.
Doctor Hill also spoke to Mayor Roy late last night by telephone, and to Mongrain.
Pastor Boeda, said Doctor Hill, was the victim of a kidnapping on March 4 when a group of Shawinigan Falls people forced him into an automobile, drove him to Three Rivers and put him on a train to Montreal. However, Mr. Boeda returned to his Shawinigan Falls post shortly afterward.
Mongrain said that when the brethren were escorted from the house at 11.30 p.m. by Shawinigan police, there were still about 1,000 persons gathered in the street.
He said the crowd was composed of men, women and children throughout the evening, but that only part of them took an active part in the stoning.
Mr. Mongrain is paralyzed in both legs and is confined to a wheel chair.
Mayor Roy said that he had been told that as many as 2,000 persons comprised the mob at its largest.
The Shawinigan police force is composed of 34 men working in three shifts, but only the night shift, then on duty, was called to the scene.
It was reported an automobile parked nearby was damaged during the stoning. Window glass in the car was broken after several bystanders let the air out of the tires.
Chief of Police Longval said that there were about 2,000 people in the crowd at its largest. He said he supervised police operations throughout the evening but that "the crowd was too large for us to handle."	[DOT]
He said four or five taxis were called at 11.30 p.m. and the brethren were herded into them. He said there were "about 40" brethren, including children. He said some were from Three Rivers.
I have chosen that report because it seems to be calm, collected and factual. I think it gives the essential details in which people might be interested in times to come. I should like to read one other statement which I think will be of value in this connection, and I refer now to the Montreal Daily Star of April 14 where a report is headed, "Attack on brethren believed made by mob in error." This report contains a statement by Dr. Arthur C. Hill,

chairman of the executive committee of the Christian Brethren Church in Quebec. An excerpt from the report reads:
Doctor Hill estimated that out of the crowd of 1,500 who stood outside the store the night of the mob assault, about 1,400 took no part in the stoning.
But the one hundred or so who did-apparently mostly young men-did a terrific amount of damage in one hour.
Further down in the report is a quotation which I think is fitting in order to estimate what occurred. I quote:
Police Chief Napoleon Longval of Shawinigan Falls reiterated today that he and his ten constables who were on the scene when the rioting took place were unable to control the mob, which was made up of men, women and children. He said a full investigation was being made, but there had been no arrests and there were not likely to be any.
I should like now to read into the record two editorials which have a bearing on this event. The first appeared in the Montreal Daily Star of April 14, and I have chosen this for obvious reasons. It reads:
A Shameful Attack
The Shawinigan mob's attack on the place of worship of Christian Brethren is a shameful act that should be repudiated by the authorities. It reflects no credit on anyone and if the mob leaders-and there must have been leaders-are allowed to go unpunished, Quebec's reputation for tolerance and fairness will suffer. On these grounds alone, but more particularly on the ground that freedom of worship is guaranteed by the constitution of this province, a full inquiry should be made into the outbreak. It should cover not only the actions of the mob but also the failure of the local police to identify and arrest a single person in a crowd that by their own estimate numbered at least 1,000 persons.
It may not be generally known-certainly it was unknown to whoever led this mob-that freedom of religion in this province rests not only on wholesome custom but on law. This is one of the few provinces in the dominion where this fundamental right is guaranteed by statute.
The enacting clause of the statute is quoted here for the benefit not only of the public but of the police of Shawinigan who are clearly ignorant of its terms and of their obligation to act under it. The Act Respecting Freedom of Worship and the Maintenance of Good Order in and near Places of Public Worship (chapter 307, revised statutes of Quebec, 1941) has this to say:
"The free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship, without discrimination or preference, provided the same be not made an excuse for acts of licentiousness, or a justification of practices inconsistent with the peace and safety of the province, are by the constitution and laws of this province allowed to all His Majesty's subjects living within the same."
This act provides penalties by way of fine or imprisonment for violations. It also places upon the local police the obligation to protect worshippers in the use of their religious premises and to arrest anyone who disturbs them in their religious exercises.
By definition of the act the premises occupied by the Christian Brethren is a church. There is nothing in the record to show that they are a harmful or provocative sect. On the contrary, there is everything to suggest that the members of this very old sect are law-abiding, peaceable citizens.

Moreover, in this province they are incorporated as a religious body and by that token if by no other should be given the protection of the law.
I thought that that editorial would be of value to those who would wish to read a report of this incident. I also have an editorial which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of April 15, 1950, reading as follows:
The Right to Worship
Wednesday night's riot in Shawinigan Falls is the most ominous of the long series of religious disturbances in the province of Quebec. Earlier mob outbreaks were usually directed against the aggressive Jehovah's Witnesses sect; reprehensible as these affairs were, they had at least some provocation. But in Shawinigan Falls the victims were a small evangelical group who, as far as the news reports show, were not annoying or molesting anyone. There would seem to have been no excuse whatever for the action of the crowd in breaking up their services and wrecking their meeting place.
One cannot help wondering if the antagonism raised in predominantly Catholic Quebec by the "witness" controversy is not beginning to take the form, in some parts of the province, of a general intolerance of Protestantism-or at least of those denominations which are too small and uninfluential to defend themselves.
This would be a most disastrous development. Canada has always prided itself, and with justice, on her tradition of religious freedom. In few countries in the world have so many religious groups been able to live together in peace and harmony. But religious peace is a fragile thing and it would not take many incidents like the one on Wednesday to sow the seeds of nation-wide distrust and ill-will.
The Quebec government has a duty to act in this matter. It should lose no time in making clear to all its people that further outbreaks of this sort will not be tolerated and that all denominations will be protected in their right to meet and worship freely. That would be the best way of making sure that the trouble spreads no farther.
I thought that that editorial from the capital of my province would be a valuable contribution to the report. Just to show how factual the Edmonton Journal is in its estimate of what might happen across the country, I think it is well to quote from a report of a charitable and moderate sermon delivered by Rev. Arthur O. Lloyd in Bell Street United Church on April 23 last week in Ottawa. The report appears on page 10 of the Ottawa Citizen of April 24 and quotes Mr. Lloyd in part as follows:
In order to understand this I have gone back to the writings of Roman Catholic leaders. The Archbishop of Westminster says: "We Roman Catholics believe our church to be the only true church and, therefore, reunion means submission to the Holy See."
The article continues to quote Mr. Lloyd as follows:
On this side cf the Atlantic, Cardinal Spellman, in an article on the Catholic position as to freedom of worship, says;
"We believe the Catholic church is the only organization authorized by God to teach religious truth and to conduct public religious worship."
The Budget-Mr. Boucher
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that the Shawinigan Falls mobbing incident and all its implications will need to be borne in mind scrupulously by every provincial representative whose heavy responsibility it will be to meet next fall to assist in drafting a suitable revision of the British North America Act. Some have thought, written and said that the Ottawa government should intervene on behalf of religious freedom in Canada. Let us solemnly warn each of those tempted to that sort of thinking. Let me suggest that they reflect what might happen if some single organization of religious worshippers were to attain dominant control at Ottawa, some organization that might not hesitate to use that power to the disadvantage of other religious organizations.
The only hope of religious liberty for our Canadian children will, and must, lie in unchallengeable provincial discretion over matters of religion.
Shawinigan Falls is a grave and portentous warning, but if the warning is heeded no ill results need accrue.
Our unhappy age had worries enough already. One could have been excused for hoping that we might have been spared the distractions accompanying religious violence. I confess that I had hoped we might. It appears that I was rather too sanguine in this respect. I claim the privilege of worshipping Almighty God according to the dictates of my own conscience, and allow all men the same privilege, let them worship how, where or what they may. I had persuaded myself that all Canadians would agree with me as regards freedom of religious worship. May I most earnestly suggest that if all organizations of religious worshippers in Canada will adopt and live by a creed similar to mine in this respect, we in our generation will have least cause for regret. '

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege and an honour for me to rise in this debate as the representative of the constituency of Rosthern. It has often been said that Canada is a difficult country to govern. In respect of no phase of our life is this more true than in the economic factors that have so much influence on our prosperity and happiness. Every province in our far-flung nation has its own particular economic issue, and even every electoral district within each province has its own economic factors. For this reason I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) very warmly. I congratulate him, not only on the budget we are discussing today but also on the manner in which he has discharged the duties of his office ever since lie assumed that high position.

The Budget-Mr. Boucher
It is a matter of great satisfaction to Canadians that he has directed the fiscal policy of our country in such a way as to distribute prosperity to all parts of Canada more evenly than has ever been done before. For this great achievement the Minister of Finance has gained the confidence of the large majority of our people. He has given to his people a high order of service in war and in peace, and I am glad to be able to tell him that millions of Canadians appreciate it.
We in Canada have some reason to be proud as we review our accomplishments. There is much yet to be done. So long as we continue to make progress, so long as we live in a changing world, there will always be need for change and reform. Our people will continue to press for, and I am sure that this government will continue to enact, that which is needed to ensure the welfare of our people. In comparison with the other nations of the world, however-and it is a fair yardstick by which to judge-we have reason to congratulate our people on their industry and sound judgment, and to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and every other minister of the government on the policies under which the achievements of our people were made possible. Under the inspired leadership of the Prime Minister our country has gained a significant measure of unity, and that has been one of the important factors in our welfare.
Rosthern constituency is populated by Canadians of many racial origins. Coming from all parts of a troubled world the people of my constituency are more deeply aware than many, because of their experiences in the old land, that our continued welfare depends upon the maintenance of peace. I know I speak for everyone in my riding when I thank the Prime Minister and the government with my whole heart because they have made the preservation of peace the chief cornerstone of Liberal policy.
The people of my constituency-and indeed this can be said of the people of the whole province of Saskatchewan-depend upon agriculture for a livelihood. While we are perhaps more directly dependent upon agriculture than are the people of the other provinces, I think it is wise for all of us in the house to realize and remember the extent to which people in all parts of our country are directly or indirectly dependent on our farms. In these days of great industrial progress in Canada it is all too easy to lose sight of this fact. Because of our direct interest it is not surprising that we from Saskatchewan give a fair share of our attention to everything affecting our great primary industry.

I support the government wholeheartedly because it has always given the interests of agriculture a prominent place in its program. We have heard a great deal from several sources, principally from the two largest opposition parties in the house, that our trade channels are threatened. This is of great interest to our farmers who must have markets for an ever-increasing production. We know, of course, that in a world that continues to progress and change we shall never have, nor do we want, static markets. What our farmers want and expect, therefore, is a government that is continually finding new markets for their products. I am sure the great support accorded this government in all the rural areas of Canada was due in notable measure to the confidence our farmers had in its marketing and trade policies. When the leaders of the opposition parties told them their markets had been lost, the farmers of Canada turned to this government because they had confidence in the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
I have spoken of Canada's magnificent industrial achievements in the last fifteen years. All Canadians are proud of the high place we have attained in the industrial world. Everyone recognizes how much of this we owe to the guidance, vision and courage of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. But the farmers of western Canada appreciate him for another reason. They appreciate him because he is not only a great believer in trade but puts his beliefs into active practice. Not only does he hold proper theories in regard to trade; he is practical, in the best sense of that word. Our farmers know that while the opposition parties are predicting blue ruin the Minister of Trade and Commerce is finding markets for our goods at fair prices. The minister is able to predict favourable conditions under this government, and his administration of the department does a great deal to make those predictions come true. The world wheat agreement and the Geneva trade agreements are important steps that indicate the road we must continue to follow, and I find that the farmers of Canada appreciate this.
The great majority of the people of Saskatchewan are proud of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture comes from our province; but, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce, he is not a provincial but a great national figure. The agricultural policies of this government are designed to encourage

every segment of this industry from Newfoundland to British Columbia. The minister's record of fifteen years of service in provincial affairs and fifteen years in the federal government speaks for itself.
In my constituency and my province we greatly appreciate the gradual improvement in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The amendments of this session will extend its benefits to many more farmers in Rosthern and other constituencies in what is known as the park area of our province. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, first passed by a Conservative government under Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and greatly extended by succeeding Liberal governments, has already improved farming in our province. The benefits of this legislation should be extended to all Canada. It would mean a great improvement in farm income and in the amenities of farm life. Within a few years the treasury would be repaid ten times over for the amounts we might spend under it.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

What they advocate would, of course, not give the farmer anything of the kind. Those conducting this campaign centre their attacks particularly on the two senior members of our government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). You cannot tell any farmer of that day that he could1 then sell his product for what he liked and to whom he wished. The farmer remembers when he had to sell his wheat on the Winnipeg grain exchange and receive as little as 23 cents per bushel. He does not remember any of the interests who now claim to work for him fighting for him at that time. He is satisfied to take his
The Budget-Mr. Boucher chance with the agricultural marketing policies of this government. He now has a chance to succeed.

The great grain-growing industry of the prairie provinces has been built upon these freight rates, which are rates bought and paid for. It must not be deprived of them now. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before commencing my remarks on the budget tonight I should like to refer to an incident which took place in the house earlier today. On the orders of the day I directed to the Prime Minister a question which I had already asked on Friday last of the government. 1 asked him whether or not it was the government's intention to give the customary official welcome or official reception to Sir Basil Brooke, the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. Perhaps I was wrong, but it did seem to me that the Prime Minister was just a little brusque in answering me when he said:	"It has not been considered." I think
most Canadians have known for at least a month that this visitor was coming. I want to say that I have no axe to grind with the Irish, whether it be in the north or in the south. I do not come from Northern Ireland, and Sir Basil Brooke certainly does not share my politics. Nevertheless, I believe that the head of any country, regardless of who he is, and particularly the head of a sister nation of the commonwealth, should be given an official and friendly reception by the government of Canada.
The Prime Minister has always been known for his broad-mindedness and for his tolerance. I certainly hope that he will not disappoint many Canadians in this connection, because I am sure that many would be disappointed if this particular representative were not given a proper reception.
Getting back to the subject before the house. The budget, which was introduced on March 28 last by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), was certainly a very different affair from the tax-slashing pre-election document which he introduced a year ago. Some people at that time described the 1949 affair as the "sunshine budget". The 1950 document, with its rather nervous recognition of more difficult times ahead, reflects anything but sunshine so far as I can see. Apparently, as somebody put it, an era has ended. Apparently the lush post-war years are behind us. Gone are the periods of heavy surpluses, of substantial debt reduction and of heavy tax cuts. On the other hand, so far as I can see there is evidence everywhere of mounting costs. I think it is conceivable that in the coming year, expenditures will reach a peacetime high. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher has held his position now for approximately four years, and in that time he has brought down, I believe, four budgets.
In the first three of those budgets the minister laid down a series of principles or precepts which he described as sound tax policy or sound budget policy for Canadians. Tonight, as we look at this budget I am reminded of some words from Shakespeare's Hamlet-
This above all: to thine own self he true,
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou canst not then be false to any man.
In analysing the current budget I propose to see whether the minister has been true to himself and to the principles which he enunciated in his first three budgets. In other words, I think it is appropriate to compare the words of the minister in 1947, 1948 and 1949 with his actions in 1950.
Principle No. 1 which was advocated in former years by the minister was this, as it is set out at page 2553 of Hansard for 1947: -we should1 aim at a surplus in times of prosperity-
And again at page 4063 of Hansard for 1948:
We should deliberately budget, as a matter of policy, for substantial surpluses in times like these.
Over the past four years, in parliament and out of parliament, the Minister of Finance has reiterated his belief time and again that in times of prosperity the budget should show a substantial surplus. Are we still in prosperous times? Most member agree, I suggest, that we are. Last year I believe the national income reached a peacetime high. I believe the forecast is that during the coming year it will be even higher.
Therefore, according to the cyclical theory of budgeting, and according to the minister's oft-expressed belief, most Canadians would have expected that the surplus in the last year would have been one of the greatest in all history. They would have expected that the surplus forecast for the coming year would also be very substantial.
What are the facts? The facts are that last year the minister did show a surplus of $111 million, but this compares with $676 million two years ago, and $595 million last year. For the ensuing year the minister forecasts only a small surplus of $20 million. Surely by the minister's own standards, that is a small, paltry surplus for a very prosperous year. And what is more, the minister knows better than anyone else in the House of Commons that probably even that amount of surplus will not be achieved, because the huge revenues are based upon a boom which is as fragile as it is unique. Then,

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher moreover, suppose that Ontario and Quebec should suddenly decide to sign a dominion-provincial tax agreement. Overnight the government would need another $120 million -six times the amount of surplus forecast.
I say, then, that in this budget, and in the one he is forecasting for the coming year, the minister has not complied with what he himself described was the first requisite of a good budget in prosperous times. He has not and is not budgeting for substantial surpluses.
Principle No. 2, as enunciated by the Minister of Finance, pertained to debt reduction. There can be no doubt as to his views in this connection. At page 2553 of Hansard for 1947 he said:
It is a sensible and far-sighted policy to reduce the national debt in good times.
He repeated that in 1948. During the past year the national debt was reduced by $111 million. But that was only a very small figure when compared with the debt reduction of the two preceding years. And next year, if we can accept the forecast and the estimates of the minister, we shall be indeed fortunate if we reduce the national debt at all. In fact, there is a very good chance that we shall probably have a deficit and increase it.
As a member of parliament I ask the minister this question: If in 1948 and 1949 it was sound budget policy to reduce the national debt substantially, why is it not sound budget policy to reduce it similarly in 1950?
Everyone knows why the minister is not doing this. Everyone knows why he is not budgeting for heavy surpluses and substantial debt reduction this year. He allowed his economic beliefs to be overridden by political concessions made to help the Liberal party win the last election. As a result of those concessions, the government today is heading straight and surely for budget trouble, the oldest and most familiar disease of governments everywhere. Despite relatively prosperous times we face, as I said a moment ago, the very real danger of a deficit in the coming year. Because last year the government sacrificed sound economic principles to party politics, Canadians today, on the verge of a recession or economic difficulties, find themselves in much the same position as an army which has shot off its ammunition before the battle. I suggest the Minister of Finance must accept a good deal of the responsibility for that dilemma.
In past budgets the minister enunciated a third principle, namely the need to bring down expenditures and practise economy. Only last October, in his 1949 budget, the

minister stated that the government was practising-and I am using his words-"the most careful economy and efficiency in all departments." He went on to say that the government "had decided on the general policy of limiting expenditures." Many Canadians wish the minister would reveal where, in particular, economy has been practised. Certainly there is not very much sign of it in the present budget.
In looking over the estimates I see that the expenditures in most departments are still mounting, and spending appears to be going on unabated. Defence expenditures, for instance, are up to the extent of $42 million; health and welfare, $45 million; the post office $3 million; resources $19 million; and labour $2,300,000. A few departments were able to cut expenses, but I think even Liberal members will admit that the over-all picture is not promising.
Speaking at Montreal a few days ago, according to a Canadian Press dispatch, the minister was rather pessimistic, when he said-
Even if further economies are achieved in administrative costs they cannot possibly alter in any significant way the scale of the budget.
I say that statement is a gesture of futility by the minister. No Canadian who examines this almost unbelievable federal budget of $2.4 billion can doubt that in this vast and unwieldy machine of administration there is a great deal of money being wasted on duplication, overlapping and inefficiency.
When Mr. Hoover in the United States investigated the affairs of the United States government he reported that two or three billion dollars could be saved without impairing public efficiency in any way. In Canada the government is making no effort at all to see whether a similar saving could be made.
The fourth principle set out by the Minister of Finance in former budgets was perhaps the most important of all. It had to do with full employment, a policy which was formulated throughout the war years. It was enunciated in this house by Mr. Ilsley, the former minister of finance, and also by the present minister. As reported in Hansard for 1948 at page 4071 the present minister said this:
All political parties and the public generally take it for granted now that governments must bear some responsibility for maintaining employment when large-scale unemployment threatens.
Year in and year out for the last five years the government has given the people of Canada to understand that now it had methods of controlling or at least alleviating an economic recession if or when it should

set in. I have heard many government supporters, whether they be from Newfoundland or from away out in British Columbia, refer glibly to a shelf of public works which would be available if or when unemployment should come. Canadians have been repeatedly assured that this time it would be different, that the government had learned its lesson from its experience during the war.
But during the last winter many Canadians received a severe shock because, overnight, upwards of 400,000 people were out of work. Overnight Canada was facing an unemployment emergency; overnight the crisis was upon us. In my perhaps biased opinion the government did not measure up to that crisis. Suddenly the large shelf of public works disappeared. Conveniently forgotten were the so-called "timing grants". Gone was any mention of the public investment program. When asked for action the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told the people not to be pessimistic; he said that pessimism might lead us into another recession. Almost 400,000 unemployed, and the only action that parliament took was to rtiodify the unemployment regulations. Those things were necessary, but at best they were only a palliative.
Today the unemployment situation is improving and it is conceivable that during the spring and summer it may get better, but how can the people of Canada have any confidence in a government which has failed to deal with the minor recession of a few years ago? How can they have confidence that it can deal with a major recession if it comes?
The figures look even blacker when we compare them with our sister dominions of New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain. On the day when we had almost 400,000 people out of work, Australia had 748 and at the same time had 107,000 jobs open for people which they could not fill. On top of that they had had a substantial immigration in the past year. In New Zealand there were less than 100 people looking for work. The record in Great Britain is almost as good. On the same date that we had almost 400,000 people out of work Great Britain had a labour force of 23 million, five times that of Canada, but had only 330,000 unemployed. In other words, where we had [DOT]! out of 100 unemployed, Great Britain had only one out of 100. I think that is a striking contrast.
What reason did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) give in his budget for the unemployment that existed? On page 1210 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
While the decline in employment as a whole has been small, the increase in unemployment has been greater, due, ol course, to the fact that the total labour force continues to grow.
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
The labour force in Australia was growing much more rapidly than the labour force in Canada. The labour force in Great Britain was growing, but still in both those countries they were able to keep full employment. That was not used as an excuse for unemployment.
What did the minister suggest in his budget as a solution for unemployment? He had a kind of fourfold program. As reported on page 1210 of Hansard he said, first, that the government should create a favourable climate for expansion and development; second, that it should plan for the best timing of its own expenditures; third, it should take the responsibility for the development of primary industries; and, fourth, it should cooperate with the provincial governments. When we boil those four points down what do they mean to the average workingman in Canada? I do not know whether the words are parliamentary, but I think it means nothing less than sweet "beggar-all".
The minister reiterated his belief that the Liberal party today was depending on private enterprise to keep full employment. In other words, the basic philosophy of the Liberal party today is back where it was in the depression years of 1934, 1935 and 1936; it is depending on private business. I wish private business could provide full employment, but I have no confidence that by itself it can.
In Great Britain, rightly or wrongly, depending upon whether we agree with their methods, the Labour government has gone a good deal further toward creating a right climate and a right atmosphere. It has met the problem of providing full employment as a matter of policy. It has met the problem with a good deal of vigour and determination and by means of taxes, government expenditures and subsidies. By directing capital investment and allocating scarce materials it has been able to stimulate industrial activity. The result of these policies is that today Great Britain has a higher ratio of employment than any nation, at least any industrial nation in the world.
In my opinion Great Britain has demonstrated that unemployment can be beaten, but it can be beaten only if there is a degree of government intervention. Surely the government must realize by this time that private business by itself cannot deal with this serious problem. I have always believed that the state owes every man the right to earn a living at fair wages. If he does not want to work, it is his privilege to starve, but the right to work is a fundamental Canadian right.

The Budget-Mr. Weaver
The Liberal party failed to subscribe to that belief in the depression and I am afraid it is failing once again to subscribe to it.
On page 1219 of Hansard the minister said:
___jf	we have to face serious difficulties we
shall find that we have never been better equipped and prepared to resolve them.
At the very moment the minister was making that boast in the House of Commons officially there were 373,000 people not working. I have heard experienced parliamentarians and newsmen say that this session of parliament has been one of the most tedious since confederation. Perhaps it is, but to me the most significant fact which has come out of this session is not to be found in the headlines, is not to be found in Hansard, is not to be found in the legislation passed. Rather it is to be found in the fact that the Liberal party has once again made a right turn. For the first time since the war the government came face to face with unemployment and the only solution was direct government intervention. But the government weighed the risks involved, and turned its back on such intervention. Not only did it fail to meet the crisis, not only did it fail to come to grips with the problem, it retreated at the first minor skirmish.
It seems to me that this budget will be remembered for two main reasons. First, because we have witnessed the death of a myth-the cyclical budget has disappeared. Secondly, it will be remembered because the Liberal party has refused to accept government responsibility for employment. The people of Canada for the time being have no choice but to await the consequences.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of hesitation that I rise to take part in this debate. This House of Commons is the embodiment of the heart and mind of Canada and it is the realization that it is my job to speak for 40,000 inhabitants of this great dominion that gives me the confidence to do so.
I have sat in this seat throughout one session and the major part of a second one carefully observing proceedings. I have observed the government and I have observed all three groups of the opposition. I have been most fortunate in the seating arrangement for by virtue of my name commencing with "W" I am one of the most junior members of the assembly and when the seats were distributed I found myself in the fortunate position of being close to the official opposition and a part of that distinguished body of government supporters sitting on your left, sir, known as the rump and directly opposite


the group of gentlemen who guide our destinies. Thus when I speak, I speak directly to them.
In these observations I have been both pleased and disappointed, pleased to find my distant impressions of the government borne out by closer observations and disappointed in the calibre of the opposition. I am one of those who believe that democracy functions best when the government is opposed by a strong opposition, strong not necessarily in numbers but strong in the insight of its criticism. Because a group small in numbers can provide effective opposition to a government strong in numbers. However, I have found that that is not the case here. Within our own ranks that informed criticism is available so that the calibre of government that the country enjoys is surpassed by no country in this world. No doubt the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) will say, "What selfadulation." Well, self-adulation or not, it is a fact. Speakers on my immediate left have risen and decried the danger of one-party government. If there were any danger, and there is not, the blame would be theirs because of their own shortcomings. They would be hurrying the introduction of such a state by the ineffectiveness of their criticism.
In his speech on the budget the financial critic of the Progressive Conservative party came up with the old cry of convertibility of currencies. He refuses to face reality. He refuses to see that exchange control did not make world conditions but that world conditions made exchange control. He insists on putting the cart in front of the horse. Let us suppose for a moment that this country, so small in numbers, should declare the pound convertible, as both the C.C.F. and Progressive Conservative parties have advocated. Our country, small in numbers, would be attempting to underwrite the economy of the whole sterling area. Not only would our mythical surpluses disappear but all the inventories from our warehouses, our stockpiles and our shelves would vanish into the sterling areas as fast as ships could transport them. Because of the United States dollar content in such a large part of the goods we make, our United States dollar and gold reserves would vanish overnight, our United States credit would be cut off and we would be bankrupt. The government would be hurled from office, and rightly so, if it were so foolish as to follow that policy. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would probably be sitting where the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) now sits, and would then fasten on us a

measure of control that would no doubt rival that of Joe Stalin. It is pure guff to talk convertibility.
The United States, with an economy thirteen times the size of ours, is the only country that is physically capable of making any currency convertible at the present time, and as soon as they fully awake to their responsibility in the world, currencies will be freed of exchange controls, and not before. In the meantime this country of only thirteen and a half million people, under the leadership of the group of gentlemen opposite me, have done wonders in interpreting the economic facts of life to the western world. Canada has been in the position of the little girl in the circus driving two huge horses, Great Britain and the United States, with one foot on the back of each. Either could hurl her to destruction, but under her skilful guidance they come safely through, and all the mumbo-jumbo about convertibility will not alter the course of events.
What I am most proud of is that the Canadian people in general and the people of Churchill constituency understand these fundamental economic facts. The proof of this is to be found in the majority that supports the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and the fact that it is my privilege to occupy a seat in this body and to have the honour of speaking here today. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have examined very carefully the budget of the Minister of Finance, and particularly the budget papers and charts of our economic activities. At first I was a little disappointed that some projects had been cut back, but on more careful examination I found that as to the amount of public money allotted to capital expenditure or development in the various departments there was an increase of approximately $74 million over the previous year. I am prepared to admit that perhaps this is sufficient for one year, having in view the large program of private expansion announced. If anything, the government has been conservative in its estimates of production for the coming year.
I also observed that in terms of our production and income we are better able to carry the national debt today than at any time since the 1920's. In addition the interest load on that debt has been progressively and substantially reduced. I would draw to your attention the most important fact that the percentage of the gross national product taken in taxation has not increased in the last twenty years. That is directly opposite to what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) would have led you to believe when he was speaking a few minutes ago. He spoke of an unwieldy budget, but it is not unwieldy at all when the government is not taking a larger percentage of the gross national product in taxation than it was twenty years ago.

The Budget-Mr. Weaver
In his speech the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) discussed again the creation of money. It was my good fortune or bad fortune, whichever way you want to look at it, to be in Alberta in the year 1933, and like many others at that time I was without a plentiful supply of money. The late William Aberhart was travelling about the province holding meetings and collecting signatures on a petition to have the then government of Alberta investigate the feasibility of inaugurating social credit theories. I attended one of those meetings, and I can remember Mr. Aberhart telling the story of Pat and Mike. Between them they had brewed a barrel of beer and they were in the business of selling it. They only had a dime in cash between them, and apparently business was very bad. They had no customers. During the course of the day Pat got thirsty. He was the one who had the dime so he passed it over to Mike and helped himself to a glass of beer. Mike then having the dime passed it back to Pat, and Mike had a glass of beer. The dime went back and forth until the barrel was empty and Pat ended up with the dime he started with.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And tight.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Aberhart did not mention that but my imagination led me to believe the same thing. Mr. Aberhart left the story at this point. What he did not say was that Pat and Mike had just as much purchasing power between them as there was beer and no more. Money had nothing to do with it. My point is that the Social Credit theorists lead themselves down the garden path by focusing their attention on money and not on production. Without production money is worthless. The hon. member for Peace River presents his argument at page 1537 of Hansard, where he says:
On many occasions my colleagues and I have reminded hon. members that during the war of 1939-1945 spokesmen for the government time and again declared to this chamber that they would let no financial restrictions interfere with the war effort. The only thing we had to consider during wartime was whether we had the manpower and the material resources necessary for an all-out war effort. Canada did not hesitate to produce ships and guns and planes and tanks and shells to the utmost of our physical capacity; and for what? For destruction. Financial cost was of little or no concern. The government saw to it that what was physically possible was made financially possible...
Then he went on to quote Professor A. F. W. Plumptre of Toronto university:
''The government can always 'get money' because it may, as an alternative to borrowing or even taxation, create the required funds. This it can easily do riowadays through the leadership of the central bank and the co-operation of the chartered banks. In this way $200 million was created in this fashion last autumn."

Then the hon. member for Peace River went on:
What for? For the war effort; not to take care of the unemployed, not to offer social security, not to close the gap between the national product and the national income, but for destructive purposes. Well, I claim that this statement . . . should serve to silence those critics of ours who are constantly making the assertion that the government can get money only from taxation or borrowing.
This statement does not silence those critics. The creation of money as advocated by the hon. member can be done, but it is only another form of hidden taxation, and the most extreme and insidious form of all. Let us assume that we have $10 worth of production, and that there is $9 of purchasing power available. Then assume that the government listens to our Social Credit friends and creates an additional $9 of purchasing power. We now have $18 of purchasing power and still only $10 worth of goods to back it up. By this indirect method the government will have taken in taxation half the goods. This type of hidden taxation has been used by unscrupulous governments many times in history; it is called inflation.
As the hon. member for Peace River indicated, it happened automatically during the war because we were destroying our production, uselessly from a peacetime point of view in that we were creating a vacuum of useful goods, but most necessarily from a wartime point of view.

speechtext:
These are my own thoughts. No government could do that unless the people desired it. I would like to see the largest possible proportion of our revenues taken in direct taxation, so we would know where it came from. Money is only goods and services produced. Our savings are the difference between what we produce and what we consume. This applies at all levels from the individual to the national. Savings take many forms. They may be stocks of grain; they may be herds of cattle; they may be homes, or stockpiles of metal; industrial plant; goods on store shelves; the surpluses that our friends of the opposition speak of, a little bit of butter, a little bit of cheese and some honey. These things are our savings; our bank accounts are only claims against these goods. It is for us to say, as citizens, what we will do with these savings. If we try to pile them up without using them they lose their value, because all but gold are perishable and deteriorate. Moths and rust will destroy them.
During the war under the leadership of our government, we as citizens said, "Let us use

these surpluses; let us produce to preserve our freedom, for if we do not preserve our freedom these savings will have no value." We wholeheartedly supported the government in that policy. In the same way, if we want what we speak of as social security, as citizens we must be willing to have the government tax our production and use it for that purpose. In that way there will be a market for our productive capacity and, as individuals, the possibility of saving will be greatly increased. We can place a proportion of our savings to the government account to be used now to provide the services we ask for, and take a claim on future production in return. This implies faith in the future and confidence in ourselves. Our savings are thus stored where moth or rust can do no damage, and where they will not lose their value.
This is the theory that was adopted by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in western Canada during the war, when he told the farmers to store their wheat in summer fallow. It is exactly the same thing. We are fortunate in having a Prime Minister and a government with the wisdom, the vision and the desire to do this in spite of the difficulties facing them in the world as we find it today.
Now let us examine what I have just said in the light of the individual. As a citizen I may hesitate to cut down my standard of living. Therefore I must increase my production to provide for those who are unable to produce because of various disabilities, including old age. This is where the government comes in; and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would speak directly to the ministers. Before doing that, however, this evening the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) said the present budget was the end of an era. Let us suppose that is so; but if it is the end of an era it is also the beginning of a new era. Speaking to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), as an average citizen I would say, "I expect you by your fiscal policies to maintain a healthy economy which will, enable me as a citizen to develop and produce to the utmost of my capacity." This I was glad to see was the announced policy of the minister, and with minor exceptions his budget supports it. A few moments ago the hon. member for Moose Jaw used some words which he doubted were parliamentary. I suggest that the words he used applied to what he was saying.
Having in mind what I just said to the Minister of Finance, I ask him to lend a sympathetic ear to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his plans for the development of the west under P.F.R.A., because
The Budget-Mr. Weaver I believe those plans to be in line with what I have been saying. I also ask him to lend a sympathetic ear to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and any plans he may bring forward respecting railway development in our great northland. The same would apply to the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters). I ask the Minister of Finance to take as his yardstick in government spending the words of an eastern farmer: "Break the back forty acres before you build a new front porch." I would ask the minister to move in this direction as far and as fast as our resources will permit. Only in this way can we supply the money for which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will be asking, with my blessing. In return I shall undertake to be responsible for explaining and justifying to my constituents the necessary taxation, even if it should call for an increase, because I believe we shall be better off under such a program.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with your permission I turn to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), even though he is not in his place. Without him the program I have outlined would be useless. I ask him, in his absence, to continue the outstanding job he has been doing in finding markets for our increased production. The Department of Trade and Commerce, which has been built up by his predecessors and added to by the present minister, is second to none in any country in the world; and I am confident that under his direction the task is within the capacity of that department. I hear the odd snicker on my left, but those words are just as true as the fact that I am standing here tonight.
I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is absent at the moment, but if he were here I would say: In 1896 his illustrious predecessor Sir Wilfrid Laurier figuratively stood in Winnipeg and looked westward at the possibilities of that tremendous store of potential wealth. Under his inspired leadership this nation experienced unprecedented development. In 1911 a different viewpoint gained control, to be followed by two world wars and the terrible depression of the thirties. In 1935 the immediate predecessor of the present Prime Minister, Mr. King, took over the helm of this country and guided it back on to an even keel and successfully steered it through the war and post-war years.

speechtext:
You, sir, stand figuratively in Swan River, in Prince Albert and in Edmonton looking northward at a treasure

The Budget-Mr. Weaver house beside which the fabulous wealth, to which the genii of Aladdin's lamp had access, was peanuts. You cannot help but feel that your destiny is to follow in the footsteps of your great French-speaking Canadian predecessor, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in developing this northland. The Canadian northwest is your oyster.
Let me tell you what lies in northern Manitoba. From Cumberland House in Saskatchewan to the north end of lake Winnipeg lies what is known as the Saskatchewan river flood plain. It was in this area that the first wheat was grown in western Canada. I should like to read to you a short quotation from a treatise on the early exploration in this area:
Whether the Saskatchewan river was reached from Lake Winnipeg or by way of Lake Manitoba and Winnipegosis is not definitely known.
The la Verendryes were followed by Louis Chevalier de la Corne who started westward in 1753 to take over the western forts which had been established by the la Verendryes. He reached the Saskatchewan river and spent time at The Pas, then Fort Paskoyac. Later he went further up the Saskatchewan and established Fort a la Corne. The same year (1753) he explored the Carrot river and the following spring (1754) seeded a few acres of land in the adjacent area, thereby deserving to be called the first agriculturist of the Canadian west. His crop gave a good yield and when he returned eastward he spoke of the excellent crop returns he had obtained in that area.
These early French pioneers were followed by the English who came into Lake Winnipeg from Hudson bay by way of the Hayes and other rivers.
For centuries the flood waters of the Saskatchewan river have been carrying the silt of the prairies to this area. At places it is 40 feet deep. It has been estimated by qualified persons that an expenditure of $20 million in drainage and flood control will bring 4,000,000 acres under the plow. The town of The Pas, Manitoba, will be in the heart of this development. This amount of land in southern Manitoba now supports a farming population of 60,000 persons. This does not take into account the secondary population that draws its wealth from those who produce the primary production. Many times this amount of $20 million is required to rehabilitate a fraction of this acreage in southern Saskatchewan. Southern Saskatchewan, of course, must be done first because when you start to harness a great river it must be done from the source; but some day this river will be harnessed.
The Nelson river, running out of lake Winnipeg, will be controlled; water that is now wasted will be diverted from the south end of lake Winnipeg into the great lakes system, and when that day comes nearly every drop of water that now falls in the Saskatchewan watershed will be used in the mid-continent. Western Canada is still in
the embryonic stage. North of the area of which I speak lies the great Pre-Cambrian shield, dotted with mines.
I have heard many suggestions since I came here, Mr. Speaker. I sometimes think that if we had a map of Canada some place in this auditorium where we could see it, it would be something that would benefit us all. When a flag for Canada is advocated, I would say that that map of Canada is sufficient flag for me. If you look at the map of northern Canada in your mind's eye, put a pencil in the midst of northern Manitoba and draw an arc around Reindeer lake and lake Athabasca and up to Prince George in British Columbia, you will be practically tracing out the route of a future railroad. I would call this to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), because it could have significance for the defence of the continent.
I have already mentioned that the west was still in the embryonic stage. I remember once reading an article describing how a portion of the shell of an egg was removed and replaced by glass, and the egg incubated. What happened hour by hour and day by day was recorded:	how first the heart, and then
the brain formed, followed by the various organs, then blood vessels and bones, until finally the chicken emerged.
The railways and transportation routes of the country are like the blood vessels forming in the development of the country. When Providence laid down the great bodies of ore that have now become our mines, He did not place them beside the cities of Montreal, Toronto and Hamilton. Those of us connected with mining who have spent so many years of our lives far from the comforts of civilization are keenly aware of this fact. These rich ore bodies call for railways which in turn bring about settlements that are not even connected with the mines, and the complete developed country finally emerges.
At Trail, British Columbia, as the ore becomes exhausted, the power that has been developed because of the ore is used in the development of a chemical industry that has become permanent. So will it be with Flin Flori in the future, drawing its power from the Churchill river at Island falls. But that time is still far in the future. In the meantime another steppingstone in this northern development is appearing at Lynn lake, pushing the frontier ever further north.
I want to take a few minutes to bring to your attention exactly what I mean when I speak of treasure in the north. The Flin Flon mine went into production in 1930 with ore reserves at that time of 19,000,000 tons. Today Flin Flon is a town of 10,000 persons.

In 1949 it produced $37 million worth of metals. It paid directly into the treasury of the people of Canada, in income taxes and ore royalties, more than $5,500,000, and indirectly another $1,500,000. Considering the 10,000 people who derive their livelihood from that mine, they have contributed from five to seven and a half times the national average towards the revenues of $2,500 million collected last year by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). In the last 20 years this mine has produced directly in metals approximately $450 million worth. This type of operation, in secondary jobs entirely away from the seat of operation, contributes about two and a half times its primary production towards the gross national product, which would raise the $450 million to over $1 billion attributable to it.
In the last 20 years that one mine has paid, directly and indirectly, almost $75 million to the federal treasury, or approximately five times the national average, based on the copulation of Flin Flon. If anyone is inclined to think that this figure of $75 million is exaggerated, I would point out these facts gleaned from the minister's budget papers. Over the last 20 years the revenue of the dominion has been approximately 15 per cent of the gross national product. It has varied little except for the war years. I have just pointed out that this one mine has been directly and indirectly responsible for over $1 billion of the gross national product, and 15 per cent of $1 billion is $150 million. That is twice the $75 million that I mentioned previously.
That $150 million is ten times the national average. In the last 20 years the gross national product was approximately $150 billion. If all the people of Canada had produced wealth at the same rate for the past 20 years, the gross national product would have been approximately $600 billion or four times what it has been; and I have not taken into account the secondary drive of primary production which would more than double the figure.
I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker, whether this is treasure or not. It is figures like these that gladden the heart of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). This is just one mine in Churchill constituency. Although it is the largest, there are other large ones such as Sherritt Gordon and the Howe Sound at Snow lake, besides other small ones; and I have already mentioned Lynn lake where some millions of dollars have already been spent on development. Now, sir, when the Minister of Transport asks you for funds to enable the Canadian National Railways to extend another artery into the northern treasure house let these figures lighten your heart and say:
The Budget-Mr. Weaver "Yes, I'll ask parliament for the money", and you will do it in the knowledge that it will be bread upon the waters returning manyfold.
There is so much to say, Mr. Speaker, about this northern constituency with its Hudson Bay railway, its ocean port, its inland fisheries, its huge lumbering industry and the rich Swan river valley that I cannot do it justice. It will be sufficient to say that this is the territory spoken of in a quotation I am about to read from an address delivered by Mr. S. W. Fairweather, vice-president, research and development, Canadian National Railways, Montreal, before the Engineering Institute of Canada and the Association of Professional Engineers of the province of Manitoba in Winnipeg, Thursday, January 12, 1950. He said:
The subject which I intend to discuss is of particular interest to those who are developing what I have elsewhere termed the "frontier fringe of Canada." In many countries the word "frontier" has a grim significance but the frontier of which I speak is not a dividing line between nations, it is a dividing line between the developed and the undeveloped. Beyond it lies opportunity, a challenge to the venturesome and a sure hope of reward to industry, intelligence and perseverance. By the definition of my term, the frontier of which I speak is not static. It is being pushed back year by year. It has receded far beyond the position it occupied along the coast and the St. Lawrence river 200 years ago. Only one life-span ago this city of Winnipeg, with all its present amenities of civilization, was on the frontier fringe. Development pressed westward from the east and eastward from the west until from ocean to ocean the natural resources of Canada were made available in a belt of varying width. Now the path of development lies northward and much of what we regarded not many decades ago as a hostile, barren waste is proving to be a storehouse of wealth-the reward of the hardy, modern pioneer. The rock drill and the mine shaft may have replaced the plow and the grain elevator as symbols of development; but whether the development is of the forest, the fisheries, agriculture or mining, the end objective must be profit to the individual and an increase in national wealth.
Suffice it to say that I once heard Mr. R. A. C. Henry, former deputy minister of railways and one of the greatest authorities on transportation in Canada today, in enumerating the goods transported over the railways of the different provinces stop when he came to Manitoba and say: "You know, I never realized before how rich Manitoba was." So, hon. gentlemen, when the government asks you for funds for the north, vote them, in the sure knowledge that you are making no mistake. In speaking of this treasure house and this wealth that has come out of the north in recent years I would mention that it was not trundled out in a wheelbarrow, as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) mentioned once before when another member was speaking of northern possibilities.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to apologize for speaking, because it is the privilege of every hon. member in this debate to rise in his place and criticize the government for its management or mismanagement of the affairs of the country, whichever it may be.
I have never hesitated in this house at any time since 1940 to rise in my place and criticize the government when I thought it should be criticized, and I am going to do it at this time. During those years I have also made a number of suggestions to the government, and I am very glad that some of the suggestions have been carried out, and very successfully, too.	.
When the budget was brought down last year an industrial worker in Peterborough, a union man, stopped me on the street and said: "Mr. Fraser, you know them down at Ottawa pretty well. Tell me this: Did these birds down there work very hard to try and reduce the income tax so that we working people could have a few more dollars to spend?" I said: "Your guess is as good as mine." He said: "Well, I do not think they worked very hard; in fact the reduction that they have made in the income tax to me is not worth any more than the value of the hole in a doughnut, because although they did reduce the income tax a fraction at the same time they are so extravagant in spending that they have increased the cost of living, and it has taken away every bit of good that the reduction in the income tax should have given us."
I met that same man last week, and he said: "Well, the budget this year is not any better, and certainly Mr. Abbott, the Minister of Finance, is trying to keep up with the Joneses with the $2,400 million budget. That man certainly cannot realize the fact that Canada is only a country of about 14 million people and we are taxed $2,400 million. You cannot expect anything else when the government or its agents hand out to people who are retiring, such as Mr. Vaughan, former


president of the C.N.R. $50,000 as an honorarium, just as a present." The same man said: "What can the average workingman on a daily or hourly wage expect?" He said: "Nothing but what we are getting, and that is just two things, high taxes and high cost of living." That is the opinion of a workingman.
In order to keep up with the Joneses this government, with the taxpayers' cash, is paying over 280 publicity agents to glorify the ministers of the crown and to build up this government. They did that before the election and they have kept at it since. They are doing it in newspaper, magazine and streetcar advertisements, and that does not include radio or films that the different departments are using. This is a fact, because I had a return tabled in my name this week, No. 102B, which showed that over $120 per hour was spent by the Canadian government on publicity, $2 a minute, and that does not cover the situation by far. This $2 a minute, or $120 an hour, goes on for every hour of every day of the week including Sundays, or 365 days of the year. As I said, this does not cover the whole story. It does not cover the offices or the cost of the rent of the offices that these people occupy. It does not cover the telephones they use, the upkeep of the offices or anything of that nature. Nor does it cover their travelling expenses. I shall have to put another question on the order paper to try to get an answer.
Then, there was a dandy on the order paper in my name today! This was just a simple little question in regard to a radio program heard over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I asked if it was a C.B.C. program and the reply is, "No information." Then, to two other questions the answers are "No information"; "no information." I shall have to put another question on the order paper on that subject, also.
Last year in a new department of government they spent $229,138 for publicity alone. As I said before, this does not cover office space, telephones and things like that. If we were to dig into that figure we would find that the department spent at least a quarter of a million dollars on publicity-and that is a new department.
I acknowledge that we do need information and publicity, and that some of the money spent for this purpose is properly spent. I want that thoroughly understood. But at the same time even government members will have to acknowledge that a great deal of this literature is nothing but a buildup for the government-political propaganda. A great deal of this stuff comes into members'

offices and is spread around the country. It just reaches wastepaper baskets and does not go any further.
All this reminds me of an election advertisement which must sound very funny to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) today. This ad, issued during the campaign, is headed, "A Word to Housewives and Homemakers", and says:
You are Canada's biggest spenders. Every week you lay out your housekeeping money on food for your families and clothes for your children.
The Conservative party has pledged itself to devalue the Canadian dollar if it gets into power on Monday, June 27. That devaluation will help a few Canadian industrialists, but it will not help you.
It will mean that a Canadian dollar will buy only 90 cents worth of goods in the United States, and that all imported goods will therefore go up in price.
All your tropical fruits-oranges, bananas, grapefruit, and so on-and your imported vegetables, will go up in price.
Your cotton goods will go up in price.
Your sugar and dozens of other foods that you use every day in your kitchens will go up in price.
Can you afford to lose ten cents on every dollar of your housekeeping money?
If you cannot, vote for the Liberal party, which gave you family allowances and has done its level best to keep living costs down.

A business firm was engaged to look into the operations of the national film board and they brought in a most comprehensive report which I hope will be acted upon. On more than one occasion I have said that business methods should be adopted in the departments of government and I mentioned particularly the national film board. In this instance it has taken the white light of publicity plus an independent business examination to disclose waste and inefficiency such as could scarcely exist in any properly managed business concern.
There are all kinds of press releases put out by the different government publicity agencies. I received one the other day from the information division of the Department of External Affairs dealing with the implications of the cold war for Canada. This particular release contained the text of a speech by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to the Canadian Club and is eleven pages long. The press covered that meeting quite fully, but there is one paragraph in this release which surely takes the cake. It reminds me of the story of Red Riding Hood where the

One aspect of that responsibility, one contribution we can make to ultimate success in the cold war is to maintain right here in Canada a strong and healthy free community in which the state remains our servant and does not become our master;
