speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening to all parties in the house I have come to one conclusion, that we are all interested in more immigration. In fact the government seems to have clear sailing in the matter of amending the immigration laws. I should like to say a few words about German nationals. It is now five years since the war ended. Some say that the subject of German nationals is a ticklish question. Why should it be? We are trying to be friendly with the western part of Germany


and are also trying to keep them from joining the communist group. How can we stop them if at this late date we call them enemies? There are a great many people in Canada of German descent, and it must be galling to them that we are still barring people of their nationality from this country.
Germans are good workers; they are honest and highly intelligent. By barring them we are losing a type of immigrant that we cannot afford to lose. Other countries are benefiting because of our immigration laws. These people are going to South America and elsewhere. German people assimilate very easily with other Canadians and take part in all our activities in the districts where they settle. If we brought them here they would not clutter up the labour market because they are mostly agriculturists. They also take pride in fending for themselves and rarely go on relief. Most Germans are religious and certainly are not communistic in their beliefs. They would be an asset to Canada. Furthermore our citizens of German origin are proud of Canada and would not easily turn to other beliefs and other ways of life. Other countries, especially the eastern block, are trying to tell them that they have something that we have not. There are great numbers of Germans in my constituency, and I have lived with them. I know what they are able to do. They have helped build up this country of ours, and most of them take pride in their work. They follow good farming practices, and intend to leave their farms to their sons in better shape than when they took them over. So let us offer them our hand in friendship and welcome them here, because we need them and they need us.
With respect to surpluses, often the opposition come up with suggestions which they think may help. I do not believe the government should throw out all those suggestions without giving them due consideration, because they may invite other suggestions, out of which we may get some solution to this problem. When an hon. member is sincere he should be given a fair hearing. With millions of underfed people in the world today, we should try in some way to help them. I have spoken with people who have been in China when famine struck that land. They have told of men going about the streets in the morning picking up the bodies of those who had died during the night, throwing them in carts and taking them to incinerators to be burned or to be buried. When we hear of such things we should be thankful that we live in a country like Canada; but we shall never be able to live in peace on this continent as long as there are hungry

people in the world. There are some things here we would like to make better, but on the whole our governments have steered the ship of state through all kinds of seas and brought it through in pretty good shape. We may still run into a few storms, but if we have faith and common sense I believe we can retain our high standard of living.
Now I should bring a matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson); that is the problem of drunken drivers on our highways, which is becoming almost our No. 1 problem. I know that to some extent it is a provincial matter, but they seem to be afraid to start anything that may have some effect on tourists coming to this country. I do not believe that would be the case, because I know a great many people today are very nervous when driving along our highways because they are afraid of meeting one of these drunken drivers. So I believe the federal government should step in and see that all the provinces have the same law. It seems that many drunken drivers get off because they are able to hire lawyers who find loopholes in the law so convictions cannot be obtained. If this parliament would bring in legislation that would permit our police to take an alcohol test, convictions would be obtained in almost all cases where drivers are under the influence of liquor. When I take my family out for a drive I do not think I should be in danger at all times because of these drunks. If they would only do away with themselves I would not worry or care, because the sooner we get rid of them the better; but they have no right to endanger the lives of others and deprive them of the pleasure of driving on our highways.
There is also another matter I should like to mention at this time; that is, pensions for the widows of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I know of a case in my own constituency of a sergeant who retired after serving on the force for thirty years and 250 days. His pension was $1,593 per annum. After retiring he came west to live in a small town because of the high cost of living. One day he suffered a stroke and died. The widow was left without a cent, and never received a nickel after her husband's death. He also left a few debts, and she had to sell some of her furniture in order to get clear. She had been under the doctor's care for most of her life, and spent considerable time in sanitariums in Ontario. She now has to work to support herself; and in order to supplement her wages a certain lodge-I do not think it would be parliamentary to mention the lodge, nor do I think I should do so-is giving her $30 per month.
The Budget

Mr. Hetland
Surely this country should give her at least what this lodge is giving her. Surely that organization should not be called upon to help support her. Hers must be a needy case for the lodge to take a hand. As it now stands, the law does not give this widow anything. I believe laws should be changed when they do not provide for cases of this kind. That law has been changed now to take care of the widows of future pensioners, but it does not provide for the widows of members who served on the force prior to March 1, 1949. According to the unwritten law I believe this widow should be entitled to one-third of her husband's pension.
There is a good deal of discussion at the present time about social security, and I believe the government is sincere in its intention to bring in such legislation after receiving the recommendations of the committee that has been set up. It has been suggested that a contributory system should be adopted. This, as everyone admits, presents many difficulties. How are we going to get everyone to contribute? How are we going to enforce payment by certain classes? It is easy to collect from the labouring people as long as the employers are willing to make the collections, but many classes do not receive wages. I believe the easiest way to obtain money for such a scheme would be through a special tax, which might be called a social security tax. This tax would not apply to food, but would apply to almost all other articles. All these things have to be paid for in one way or another. If a man wants to buy a car or a yacht he can always pay a little more by way of social security tax. In my opinion this would be the fairest kind of tax, and would reach most people able to pay. I believe a majority of our people would welcome a tax of this kind, as long as they knew it meant security and hospitalization when they needed it. Further, they would realize that we cannot get something for nothing, and that the more security they wanted the more it would cost them. There would be less criticism of the government in power, and much less work in administration.
With respect to the international situation, I believe that as soon as possible we should recognize communist China, and I believe this government will do that when it sees fit. If we showed the people of China that we wish to be friendly it would not necessarily be a sign of weakness. It might well be a sign of strength and confidence. For ages the Chinese people have been living under governments that have been corrupt in every way. Can we blame them when they accept
1848	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. A. Gauthier doctrines that promise them a certain standard of living? If we show a friendly hand, surely it will do more good than harm; and we have nothing to lose.
China with her millions of people could be a wonderful market for our products, and no effort should be spared to gain her confidence. China has a great many things that we could exchange for our goods, and thus avoid currency difficulties. India is another country that we should help. Otherwise, communism has a good chance of getting a foothold there.
In conclusion I might say that the future does not look too dark. I believe that we shall be able to cross our bridges when we come to them. We certainly are going to make mistakes, because no government is infallible. I believe, however, that the people of Canada have confidence in this government and that, whatever problems arise in the future, we shall be able to meet them with courage and fortitude so that we shall be able to continue our high standard of living and also to retain the friendship of other lands so that we can talk more of peace and less of war.
I do not believe that the people of any country want war. We in Canada certainly do not. We should at all times try to show the people of the world that we are only too glad to extend to them the hand of friendship and love.

speechtext:
I deem it my duty to take part in this debate. Since my last speech in the house, important events have happened. I am pleased to congratulate the government on the wise measures they have adopted particularly with regard to unemployment insurance for lumbermen. At the very beginning of this session, the government extended the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act to this class of workers. They even went one step further and made these provisions retroactive.
The lumbermen need some protection against the hazards of an industry which remains unstable and seasonal in character, in spite of certain tendencies in the opposite direction. In extending the provisions of the act to lumbermen, the government has shouldered its responsibilities and protected an impressive number of workers in my riding. I am happy, on behalf of this class of worker, to thank the government for this measure of justice and foresight.
[Mr. Hetland.l

The various amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act have attained their aim in partially decreasing seasonal unemployment, which hits more severely the lumbering industry.
The Aluminum Company intends to undertake in the near future important projects in the Chute au Diable district, which will solve for the present the problems of the working class.
But the farming class also has its problems. Since the government is keeping aware of the needs of every section of the Canadian people, and in view of the favourable way in which my requests have been received in the past, I am again confident in pleading the cause of our farming people.
Dairy farming is the basic industry in the constituency of Lake St. John and the most important one to the farmers. It is therefore not surprising that they should be highly interested in the price of milk, butter and cheese. In the past, owing to the excellent agricultural policies of the government, they have obtained a fair price for these products. The present instability of the market and a decline in the price of these products have brought about some degree of uneasiness among farmers. The price of feed and fertilizers remains high. It is easy to understand why the possibility of price gaps and the prospect of producing without profit, if not at a loss, should worry our farmers. I bring the matter of feed and fertilizers more particularly to the attention of the government so that every possible means may be taken to put these products within the reach of our farmers.
Through clubs in each parish of my constituency, the Union catholique des cultivateurs have asked me to urge the government to maintain floor prices on agricultural products, and on cheese in particular, at last year's level.
I take pleasure in acting as mouthpiece for the agricultural groups of the U.C.C. Agriculture is the Canadian economy's most stable industry. By helping to maintain the prosperity of the farmers, the government ensures the prosperity of the Canadian nation.
During the last session, Mr. Chairman, I urged old age pensions for all at age 65, without a means test. I am happy to note that the hon. the Minister of National Health and Welfare has moved that a committee be set up to make a complete investigation of the situation and to advise the government on

the policy to be followed. This committee will be given an excellent opportunity to suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that steps be taken to protect those citizens who are invalids and those who suffer from some congenital or accidental infirmity. That is one social security measure that deserves to be carried out in the near future and the government would be well advised to give the matter its closest attention.
May I be permitted now,-and at this stage of my speech I am happy to see that the hon. the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is in his seat,-to deal with a matter close to the heart of the people of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district, namely, the building of a railway between Chibougamau and Lake St. John. As a matter of fact, it is our duty, as Canadians, to encourage the development of our natural resources and the building of a railway between Chibougamau and Lake St. John. The government can make no mistake, since this mining area is already, without any doubt whatsoever, one of the most promising mining centres in Canada.
The natural economic outlet for the Chibougamau district is lake St. John. Historical rights, geographical reasons and economic interests all justify the building of a railway line up to lake St. John. Since 1897 explorers have always reached Chibougamau through lake St. John. As a matter of fact, even before the Abitibi district had been heavily settled, a proposal for a railway had been studied at lake St. John and submitted to the proper authorities. All those who are in good faith- and that is the case of everybody in the Abitibi district-admit the soundness of the demands made by the people from the Saguenay.
Hydroelectric power, the means of transportation such as planes, good roads and the water route of the Saguenay, all these reasons favour the selection of lake St. John as the natural outlet for the rich Chibougamau district. The wealth of a province should serve that province first, and those who suggest the building of a railroad to northern Ontario have surely forgotten that it would be wiser to keep for the lake St. John workers, and therefore, for the province of Quebec, the handling and processing of ore, the development of which has been made possible by the natural resources of the lake St. John district and the initiative of its people.
The Budget-Mr. A. Gauthier
This project would also help agriculture, colonization and the lumber industry in the district between St. Felicien and Chibougamau. In the interest of the district, of the province of Quebec and of the country I would request the authorities concerned, that is the government, the hon. Minister of Transport and the Canadian National Railways, to give careful consideration to the building of a railroad between Chibougamau and lake St. John and to carry out this project in the near future.
I was speaking a moment ago on the subject of the Canadian nation. I would like before concluding to speak of one of its most essential characteristics, namely its sovereign rights.
During the last electoral campaign, I stood, like the Prime Minister himself, for a really and truly independent Canada, a Canada owned and governed by Canadians at all levels of authority. What I was saying then was not the result of political expediencies, but the expression of a deeply-rooted conviction.
The results of the federal-provincial conference of January filled me with pride and confidence in the future. It is to be hoped that the interested parties will continue to work in the same constructive spirit and with the same understanding of the various points of view of the different parts of the country. This moderation, understanding and enlightened patriotism will continue, I hope, to govern the future negotiations so that we may have a truly Canadian constitution which will be acceptable to all Canadians.
I regret that I was not in this house on April 17 when the hon. member for Ottawa East suggested that a committee be set up in order to select a distinctive national flag. I am glad however that the budget debate is flexible enough for me to deal with this question. We are at a momentous period of Canada's constitutional development and this is a most opportune time to give our country a distinctive Canadian flag.
The nationals of a truly sovereign country are duty bound to insist upon a symbol of their common ideals.
Our national unity, our people's aspirations, our past history, our soldiers' sacrifices on the battlefields, our political freedom, won at the price of heavy sacrifices, our national prestige, our genuine patriotism, are many reasons, Mr. Speaker, which call for an immediate and final decision about a truly Canadian flag.
Much has been said about national unity. In my opinion nothing is better calculated to cement national unity than a flag which can

The Budget-Mr. Fulford truly and upon occasion serve as a rallying standard tor all Canadians. The citizens of this country are proud to belong to this happy and fortunate Canadian nation. The best way to show this common pride is to see to it that it takes shape in an exclusively Canadian symbol.
What I have just said of the flag may be applied also to the national anthem. "O Canada" by Calixa Lavallee, in its English and French versions, would certainly be the happiest and most logical choice. It is now accepted in every part of this country and all that is required now to ensure its definite acceptance and confirmation is an official declaration by the government.
Mr. Chairman, this spirit of Canadianism and enlightened patriotism shown by the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues give me reason to expect, in the not too remote future, a complete and unrestricted national sovereignty. A natural and indispensable complement to this sovereignty logically and sensibly calls for the prompt adoption of a truly Canadian flag and a national anthem. Around this flag we shall build together, in a spirit of unity and brotherhood, a prosperous, independent Canada, a true world power.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so much has already been written and said about the budget that it is not my intention in this debate to criticize nor to applaud the efforts of our genial and very capable Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott); but I would like to remind hon. members to compare our financial position with that of any of the other western democracies. When we observe our great neighbour to the south piling up annual deficits running into billions of dollars each successive year we can be quite satisfied with the amounts that have been written off our national debt in spite of considerable tax reductions since the war; and, furthermore, that Canada's budget again anticipates a surplus of some $20 million of revenue over expenditure with virtually no change in the tax structure.
What interested me particularly in the minister's carefully prepared presentation were two remarks pertaining to our foreign trade, and I shall quote him as reported in Hansard of March 28, 1950, at page 1208:
Frankly we have been a little disappointed in the apparent inability of overseas countries to resume their traditional share of our import market during the past year.

Later on the same page appears this statement:
Our overseas exports as a whole, however, were down by more than $100 million in these four months, and our overseas imports down by $12 million.
The four-month period referred to was November, 1949, to February, 1950, inclusive. Considering the quota and monetary restrictions so prevalent throughout the western world, but especially with regard to our traditionally best customers within the British commonwealth of nations, it is really a glorious achievement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and Canadian industry that our foreign trade is being maintained at such a high level.
The fact that our exports to the United States are ever increasing should be most gratifying, because the goal may soon be reached which we have been striving to attain for so many yars, where the balance of trade may be equal or even in Canada's favour.
No one who saw the motion pictures shown in the railway committee room last month of the stupendous development in the iron ore areas of Labrador, or read of the great potential oil fields of Alberta and Saskatchewan, could help being impressed with the glorious future that lies ahead of us. We must never let ourselves become satisfied, however, because self-satisfaction leads to complacency, and real progress can only be attained by continually striving to expand our domestic and foreign markets.
Private enterprise has done a magnificent job in Canada, and private enterprise will continue to serve our best interests. While I am on the subject of private enterprise, Mr. Speaker, may I ask how these 13 members of the Conservative party are going to explain their position of having voted for the amendment of the C.C.F. leader to the resolution of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on April 18, an amendment which would have reimposed wartime controls on industry? In fact, one of the interesting features of this session has been the number of times the Conservative party has upheld motions and amendments of the C.C.F. party. Sometimes you would almost think that they were one.

I believe our government can assist both farmers and industrialists by negotiating more multilateral trade agreements, by granting further reciprocal arrangements, and even by barter with certain nations if the occasion should warrant such action.
At this point I should like to pay special tribute to the personnel of our diplomatic corps and of our trade commissioners, and to urge the government to increase the number of our Canadian offices abroad. I have been associated with a business that has connections in practically all democracies of the world, and I can assure all hon. members through you, Mr. Speaker, that it is impossible to calculate the aid that Canadian firms have received from our trade commissioners. The diplomatic prestige of Canada is out of all proportion to our population, and too much credit cannot be given to our Department of External Affairs for the calibre of the men chosen and trained to represent us in our embassies and legations. I should like to offer as a suggestion that Canada's trade commissioners and diplomatic corps be more closely integrated even to the point of complete amalgamation so that promotions can be made from one branch of the service to the other.
I should now like to point out a certain area where latent markets do exist that have not as yet been fully realized, or perhaps I should say where our trade is being severely curtailed. We must bear in mind that Marshall aid money to Europe will end in two years, and as a result a large source of United States dollars now supplying Canada will then cease to exist. We must be prepared for this eventuality, and therefore any latent markets must be surveyed and developed. I refer to the possibility and advisability of greatly improving our trade relations with the British American territories from Bermuda in the north to British Guiana in the south.
I shall now digress for a moment to explain the financial position of other dominions within the commonwealth. At the conclusion of the first world war there were vast German possessions in Africa and the south Pacific which were surrendered under the terms of the peace treaty. The Union of South Africa gained a mandate over South West Africa which embraces an area of over 317,000 square miles with a population of 318,000, of which nearly 31,000 are of European
The Budget-Mr. Fulford extraction. Although certain local administrative and legislative powers were granted this territory, the Union of South Africa under article 2 of the mandate-
-shall have full power of administration and legislation over the territory subject to the present mandate as an integral portion of the Union of South Africa and may apply the laws of the Union of South Africa to the territory, subject to such local modifications as circumstances may require.
Thus, our sister nation within the commonwealth obtained not only a great additional territory but also a tremendous potential market in which to buy and sell.
New Zealand first obtained territorial expansion in 1901 when Great Britain under the Boundaries Act of 1895 allowed another sister dominion to annex the Cook islands, a group of fifteen islands in the south Pacific and Niue with a total area of about 200 square miles and a combined population of over 18,000.
When western Samoa was surrendered by Germany after the first world war, New Zealand was given the administration of this territory which consists of two main islands and several smaller ones with a combined area of about 1,200 square miles and an estimated population of over 71,000 according to the 1947 census.
Trade with these territories has shown a consistent upward trend with exports showing a favourable balance over imports for some years. This trade is strictly regulated by the New Zealand government and the importation and exportation of goods is permitted only under licence with countries other than New Zealand.
Ross dependency was granted New Zealand in 1923. This territory in Antarctica has an area of 175,000 square miles but is completely uninhabited. It affords land bases for whaling operations where an annual fee of 200 pounds is charged for each expedition and a royalty of 2s. 6d. for each barrel of whale oil produced.
Of all the commonwealth nations Australia has gained the most in additional territories being brought under the federal administration. Norfolk, a tiny island between Australia and New Zealand, was created a distinct and separate settlement in 1856 under the jurisdiction of New South Wales, and in 1913 was accepted as a federal territory of Australia. Small as the island is, with an area of only 8,500 acres and a total population of 938, it has proven to be a valuable tourist resort and land station for the "All Red Cable" from Great Britain to Australia and New Zealand via Vancouver.
Papua was the first territory of treaty importance to come under the authority of

Mr. Fulford the Australian commonwealth, when in 1906 it was accepted by proclamation by the government. It has an area of over 90,000 square miles comprising 87,000 on the main island and 2,800 on adjacent islands. The official population is estimated at 300,000, of whom only 3,000 are whites. Much of the revenue of the territory is raised from import duties and Australia grants free entry into Australia of certain goods produced and imported direct from Papua. The trade statement of 1941 shows imports exceeding exports but Papua has large mineral deposits and potential natural resources which remain to be developed and which include gold and copper.
In September 1914 the acting governor of German New Guinea capitulated to the officer commanding a naval and military expedition sent from Australia, and thereafter the territory was under military administration until the establishment of civil government in 1921.
The territory has an area of about 93,000 square miles comprising northeast New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomon islands. The total population is over
680,000	of whom only 3,400 are white.
The territory is rich in natural resources and the ratio of exports to imports averages over three to one with Australia obtaining the vast bulk of both exports and imports.
Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand have joint jurisdiction over Nauru, formerly part of the protectorate of German New Guinea. The island has only an area of 5,200 acres with a total population of 2,800 but valuable deposits of phosphates are worked with the entire normal annual production of over one million tons going to Australia and New Zealand. It may be of interest to note that although the territory is under a joint administration the complete authority is vested in the federal government of Australia.
Mr. Speaker, at no time has Canada sought or been offered additional territory beyond the confines of British North America; nor do I suggest for a moment that we should even make such a demand. I do feel very strongly on the subject, however, that we are being deliberately refused the right to trade with the British West Indies on an equitable basis and I am .assured many West Indies business firms resent the fact that their markets are being denied us. What good are the preferential tariffs granted us if import and export restrictions are created against us under the guise of currency controls? As I have pointed out South Africa, New Zealand and Australia have all been
ceded territory which virtually amount to colonial possessions and from which they derive no uncertain trade advantages.
No one could conceive of Canada having any ambitions of colonial expansion, although from time to time one hears the suggestion that the British West Indies come into our confederation as the eleventh province. The difficulties in this are so manifold that I am afraid such a suggestion is impractical but by no means impossible should the colonies themselves express such a desire.
At present there are no less than nine separate territorial administrations each charging customs duties against the others, so trade between them is carried on in a most uneconomical way. Of the nine colonial groups British Guiana and British Honduras with a total area of nearly 92,000 square miles are on the mainland of South America and Central America respectively.	The
other seven are islands or groups of islands consisting of Bermuda, Bahamas, Jamaica-including the Turks, Caicos and Cayman islands, -Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, Leeward islands and Windward islands with a total area of about 12,500 square miles. The combined estimated population in 1946 of all nine administrations was nearly 3 million of whom the vast majority are of African origin. In fact living conditions are exceedingly low in the British West Indies compared to our standards, and purchasing power is correspondingly meagre. An examination of the West Indies Year Book for 1947-48 shows that imports exceed exports in almost every colony, which is not a healthy condition and one which must be remedied by the building up of local enterprises.
I might say at this point that in the case of trade with Canada at the present time our imports from the British West Indies exceed our exports. I have been told by travellers and others that much must be done to modernize plant equipment and that modern electric power plants are a vital necessity. The Canadian Department of Trade and Commerce is fully cognizant of the trade possibilities existing in the British West Indies and has accomplished a great feat in increasing our trade to the extent shown by the figures published by that department.
I shall not give the annual figures, but it is interesting to compare 1938 with 1948. In the former year our total trade with the British West Indies amounted to approximately $34 million of which $14 million were exports and $20 million imports. In 1948 this trade figure had increased to $100 million, of which $58 million were exports and $42 million imports. In 1949, when Great Britain severely restricted imports from Canada, the

total trade figure had increased to $105 million, but the trend was completely reversed as regards exports, which had fallen to $43 million, whereas our imports had increased to $62 million, a difference of nearly $20 million in favour of the British West Indies.
An honest effort is being made by Canada to increase purchases from the British West Indies as is evidenced by the fact that virtually all our sugar requirements for 1950 are to be purchased from that source. We have further increased our imports of canned citrus fruit juice and I believe there are still more products that we could buy from the same source, such as cotton, coffee, coconut oils and petroleum, but in return positive guarantee must be given that Canadian dollars so earned will be used to acquire Canadian agricultural products, machines of production, and electrical equipment. At present all dollars earned in the Caribbean area are transmitted to London to be put in a general pool for the entire sterling area of the commonwealth, a policy which our government should use pressure to see is abolished or greatly modified by the British colonial office.
Canada and Canadians are popular with the people of the West Indies. For the last two years of the second world war the Brockville Rifles were garrisoned on the island of Jamaica where the battalion was treated with respect and held in high esteem in spite of the fact that our men were there to maintain law and order. There is undoubtedly unrest in many parts of the colonies which is natural where people are forced to live in poverty and want. That this unrest is real can be best shown in the editorials and news stories appearing in the leading papers of the various colonies. I have a number of editorials right here on my desk, but I do not intend to quote them all. However, I should like to quote in its entirety an editorial from the Sunday Guardian, Port of Spain, Trinidad, of January 15, 1950, which summarizes the general trend of thought in the colonies. This editorial reads:
Give us Economic Union With Canada
The West Indies sugar talks in London have ended on a note of pessimism contrasting strangely with the buoyant hopes aroused by the United Kingdom government's August, 1949, statement. It seemed then that we were assured a long-term agreement and special consideration with regard to quantities in view of the vital place the United Kingdom government acknowledged sugar to hold in the West Indian economy. These hopes have been *crushed and the B.W.I. deputation are leaving the mother country today without an agreement. What is more, the ministry of food has demurred about the talks being postponed to allow time for consultations in the West Indies before acceptance of the United Kingdom terms.
Much could be written about this inglorious ending to the sugar talks, whereby the West Indies
The Budget-Mr. Fulford are confronted with a cut in their export quota after the existing contract expires in 1952, while Britain in effect is offering Cuba and Santo Domingo a market for 500,000 tons a year. But invective can be kept for another occasion. The big question is, what are the West Indies going to do about the sugar situation? It is evident we can no longer rely on the mother country for reciprocal treatment of our major agricultural product, in spite of the high prices and marketing monopoly we are forced to concede to British goods. From now on the West Indies must depend less on Britain and turn their eyes to another quarter. Where better than to the Dominion of Canada, with which we have had long and cordial economic and cultural relations?
In view of the failure of the sugar talks, the Hon. Dr. P. V. J. Solomon has given notice in the Trinidad legislative council of a motion urging that trade negotiations be instituted for disposal of our exportable products in countries other than the United Kingdom, and asking for a larger allocation of hard currency for purchases outside the sterling area. While we are in full sympathy with the motion, it should be clear that more dollar exchange would make little difference to the West Indies today because of devaluation. The suggestion for trade discussions with other countries, however, ought to be acted upon.
The possibility of an agreement with Venezuela for the purchase of Trinidad sugar is already being canvassed, and the consul general for that country in Port of Spain seems hopeful that a contract will be negotiated. This might indicate a line of action which could profitably be pursued. Much more than this is needed, however, if Trinidad and the other British Caribbean colonies are to achieve the economic stability which can only come from assured export markets and reasonable financial returns. Instead of asking at this stage for more dollars, the B.W.I. should unite in sending a strong representative deputation to Canada to sound out the prospects for some form of economic union with that dominion.
This idea, in fact, is inexorably taking shape as an imperative necessity for the British Caribbean. The benefits of having our security linked with the Canadian dollar are evident, and Canada has shown an interest in these colonies which leads us to hope she may be willing to consider such an arrangement. The West Indies offer a sizeable market for Canadian goods, and these colonies have products to sell in which the dominion is interested. Then let the West Indies act at once and together in this matter. Let there be a vigorous stir throughout the British Caribbean to go to Canada and place our cards on the table, face up. There is nothing to prevent our doing this; on the contrary, the sugar ultimatum from London drives us to it as a means of simple self-preservation.
As you will see, the present trend oi thought is for closer economic unity with Canada and I know of no better time than now to press for this aim. I understand that the Canadian-British West Indies trade treaty is soon to come up for renewal and certainly the best reciprocal terms should be arranged along with the demand that the British West Indies be allowed to purchase at least as much from us as we have been buying from them. An unfortunate economic situation exists amongst the nine different colonial administrations whereby each has its own customs duties- and separate income taxes as well-which are levied not only against nations outside the Caribbean but also against each other.

The Budget-Mr. Fulford A system of uniform tariffs must be adopted if the West Indies are to achieve the greatest economic stability and at the same time create equal opportunities for Canada's trade with each colonial administration.
That a substantial market for our agricultural products exists is evidenced by the fact of our exports to the British West Indies during the war, and that these imports into the West Indies area are being seriously curtailed now there can be no doubt. Because of the currency restrictions many articles such as wheat flour, potatoes, butter, cheese, dried fish and evaporated milk are now being replaced by similar products from New Zealand, Australia and other soft currency countries. In the particular case of evaporated milk I know positively that importers have been issued instructions to buy this product from Holland. Naturally this is resulting in the loss of a valuable market to the farmers and manufacturers of this Canadian commodity. Butter is another dairy product which Canada could supply but it is now shipped halfway around the world from New Zealand to the markets of the British West Indies.
That the West Indian himself is not in accord with the British policy is forcibly expressed in a recent prize winning calypso song. I might explain that the calypso song is a method by which the West Indian expresses his thoughts and political views, and I should like to quote one of these songs taken from page 27 of the Canadian edition of Time of February 27, 1950. There are prizes given each year for the best calypso song, and I now wish to quote the one that won the prize for 1950 in the island of Trinidad. The title is:
Give up the West Indies, Britain The text of the song is:
In England the people live happily They get doctor, medicine and dentist free . . . While down here three-quarters of the population . . .
Dying out from disease and malnutrition . . .
I'm warning Great Britain, don't leave us for long
Or they'll wake up one morning and find these islands gone.
If they won't help us in our difficulties Why don't they give up the West Indies? f don't think I am so loyal today,
I don't mind this island being taken by the U.S.A., For one thing at least I feel confidentially,
We would sing our native songs in tranquillity.
The thoughts contained in this song are worthy of most serious consideration not only by the British but particularly by Canadians. We have proven that we are ready and willing to furnish what is most needed to help the British West Indies in supplying them with those commodities which will do much 
to give them economic stability. We definitely do not wish territorial expansion but in all justice we should be given the right to trade with those who wish to trade with us. It is a known fact that we have much to offer them and if we can help them by our efforts we shall do much to raise their standards of living, thus increase their purchasing power, and at the same time quiet the unrest that seems to be becoming so general throughout the colonies.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that these are unfair questions to ponder. What would be the reactions of the Afrikaans if South West Africa were forced by the colonial office to restrict its imports from the Union of South Africa? How would Australia feel if she were suddenly cut off from Papua and New Guinea? Would New Zealand stand idly by if trade privileges were curtailed with the Cook islands and western Samoa, or if she could no longer collect fees from the whaling expeditions in the Ross dependency? I am sure the answers to all these questions would be the same, and I am equally certain violent dissension would result. True, the matter of Canadian dollars versus pounds sterling is involved. But, Mr. Speaker, we are at the moment buying more from the West Indies than we are selling, and I repeat that we should be allowed to balance our trade on a fair and equitable basis.
I can only say in conclusion that I feel great mutual benefit will result if we can attain the right of freer trade relations with all sections of these territories comprising the British West Indies and stretching right from Bermuda to British Guiana.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought I should take part in the debate tonight because two or three times lately I have been taken for a senator, and I do not think any harm will be done if I get a few lines on Hansard. About two weeks ago I had to visit one of the departments, and I was talking with a gentleman there who persisted in calling me "senator". He kept referring to me as "senator", and when I was leaving he said, "I will write you and let you know about that, senator." I said, "I am sorry, but I am not a senator and I hope I shall never be." I thought perhaps it would be just as well for me to get a few more speeches in Hansard and then I would not be taken for a senator. The only reason I know of why I might be taken for a senator is that my uncle was a member of the Senate some twenty years ago. I believe he was there around 1934.
There are two or three observations I should like to make with regard to the budget.

The first is that the minister gave us a figure of 12 per cent representing salaries and wages that the government pays. I take it that refers to the salaries and wages of permanent and non-permanent civil servants. I thought it was a fairly reasonable figure, and I came to the conclusion that the civil service was giving the taxpayers pretty good value for their money, provided that the figure of 12 per cent is what I think it is. It would be very interesting to take the budget of 1938 and see how it compares with today as to that figure. I would think it would likely represent more than 12 per cent of the budget in those days.
We often hear civil servants referred to as people who do not work very hard, that they are a leisurely crew and all the rest of it. Personally I think that just the opposite is the case. I have found these ladies and gentlemen to be most courteous and I believe they are a hard-working lot. Some of them work a lot harder than I would care to. Therefore I do not think we are overpaying our civil servants at all. I do not think it is the civil servant who is wasting the taxpayers' money. It is our Liberal politicians. I do not say that the cost of government could not be cut down even lower than 12 per cent. Goodness knows we have a lot more departments of government and ministers now than we ever had before. If you go back to the year 1911, we had seven million people in Canada at that time. It is now 1950, and I do not believe we have more than thirteen million people today. Yet we have many more departments and ministers to govern the country now than we had then, and how much better are we being governed? I do not think the average citizen is getting any more help from the government than he did in 1911. It is time that a lot of the departments that are not absolutely necessary should be done away with in the interests of economy. I do not want to lay any blame on the civil servants. I think the figure of 12 per cent of the budget for the payroll which the minister gave us is not out of the way for everything that civil servants are called upon to do today.
There is another point the minister mentioned that I did not like at all. He did not think the cost of running the government could be cut below the $2,400 million he has estimated for the coming year. He said he thought expenditures had been pretty well pared, and did not see how they could get under that figure. Most of us do not want to have to go on paying the heavy taxes we pay today, so that statement by the minister was not very promising. I am not
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield saying we are going to have a recession, but if we should our revenues will fall off materially, both from corporation and income taxes. If that should happen we would be faced with two alternatives, either deficit financing or increased taxes; and, as I have said, most of us are tired of paying high taxes. After all, who pay most of the taxes? It is the men with incomes of $3,000, $4,000, $5,000, $6,000 or $7,000 a year, and today those men are having a pretty hard time to get along. Any thought of having to pay higher taxes certainly does not make them very happy; so if the minister is right it seems to me our only hope for lower taxation is through a greater inflation or an expanded economy. That may be pretty hard to bring about, because we are pretty well up the ladder at the present time, so I certainly hope the government can find ways of reducing its expenditures rather than raise taxes any higher.
I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is in his place; and speaking for my province of Nova Scotia I want to thank him for the interest he has taken in our marshlands. He set up a commission headed by engineers which has outlined a program to reclaim our marshes. That will be of great help to us in Nova Scotia because, as I have said many times, we have not too much land suitable for farming. Much of it is submarginal and good only for growing spruce trees and things of that kind. The farmland that was always the most profitable is in the counties of Cumberland, Colchester, Hants and Kings, where there is a great deal of marshland. When you drive through those sections of the province it is easy to see that they are much more prosperous than the inland or upland farms. Really I do not know how many of the people on the upland farms have been able to live all these years. Certainly they have had a very hard time. We in Nova Scotia do not produce nearly enough to meet our own needs, and we hope the minister may be able to bring in a few Danish and Dutch farmers for settlement in these new areas, because they are accustomed to working that kind of land.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is not in his place, but I am going to mention the matter of the Canso bridge. I see the government has said that this bridge cannot be built because the trans-Canada highway requires a 24-foot roadway across it. To me that excuse seems pretty lame. I think that Canso bridge was just an election promise for last year, and I do not believe the government ever had any intention of building it. Anyone taking the trouble to study the tides and currents and ice and other hazards in the
1856	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield strait of Canso can easily understand why a low level bridge fourteen or fifteen feet above high water level cannot be built. The ice would pile up on the piers and take out that bridge the first spring it was there. They built a bridge something like that out in Vancouver and have had a great deal of trouble with it ever since. If they had that much trouble out there, how much more trouble would they have in the strait of Canso? Some day a bridge will be built, but I am afraid it will cost a great deal more than the proposal put forth by the government. Personally I never looked for the bridge to be commenced under the plans outlined in the house by the minister.

The next thing I want to talk about is the matter of freight rates. I do not know whether we are allowed to speak about freight rates at this time; but in any case it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
